In Section 7, with $\mu=\lambda_{j-1}$, the full normalized interval has length at most $CL_{j+1}^4$, $L_{j+1}\le(\log\mu)^2$, and $\delta$ is bounded by $\mu^{-1/16}$ times a fixed power of $\log\mu$. An estimate $CT^C\delta$ is therefore absorbable uniformly in the induction; an estimate exponential in $T$ would not follow from these bounds.

r5-reference-reference-peak-overview|Tor.annotation: Set $v=\sqrt\varepsilon\,\tau$. Then $\int_0^\infty\cos\varphi\,d\tau=\varepsilon^{-1/2}\int_0^\infty(1+v^4/4)^{-1/2}\,dv$. Its tail after $\tau_m$ is at most one. In Equation (2.14) the correction $e$ changes this integral by at most $O(\sqrt\varepsilon)$, and the square-root prefactor costs $\tfrac12\log\varepsilon+O(1)$ in the logarithm. Thus most of the logarithmic gain is accumulated on the turning scale $\varepsilon^{-1/2}$, although the maximum is later, at $\tau_m\asymp\varepsilon^{-1}$.

r5-reference-relative-comparison-overvie.annotation: The comparison does not estimate the difference of two large amplitudes in absolute size. It divides both by the positive reference amplitude and measures the remaining direction error by $l$ in Equation (2.15). In the reference equations $l$ can only decay, and the variation it produces in $h$ is bounded by half its decrease in absolute value. This gives a bounded forward propagator before any perturbation estimate is made.

The estimate on the scaled quotient $q=\alpha_1/\alpha_2$ is important even when the physical velocity direction is nearly $E_2$: multiplication of its small $E_1$ component by the preceding shear leaves an order-one contribution to $f_2$ in Equation (2.20). The other conclusion of Lemma 2.6, the bound for the propagator on the entire transverse plane, is used in Section 5 to estimate forced oscillatory corrections relative to the growing seed.

r5-reference-couplings-overview|TorusEul.annotation: The first new coupling must stay positive even before the crossing. Indeed $p_{\rm w}=2\nu_+|\mathbf a|/|k|$, so the leading affine pressure Hessian has central eigenvalue $-2\nu_+|\mathbf a||k|$ when $F'(0)=1$. The localized construction uses the same sign on the envelope and the shallow negative part of $F_h'$ to bound the Hessian from above (see the proof of Lemma 5.9). This bound is needed to solve the mean correction for the next parent.

additive.prescribed-wave-data|TorusEuler.annotation: The equations here only use the gradients at a fixed particle, not an affine solution of Euler on an open set. In Section 7 oddness fixes the particle at zero, and for wave $j$ the older gradient is $B=\nabla U_{j-2}(t,0)$ while $M=\nabla U_{j-1}(t,0)$. The error $E_c$ accounts for the difference between the latter gradient and the older gradient plus the principal shear of wave $j-1$.

r2a1.wave.gradient|TorusEuler.MovingWave.annotation: In units of $r$ the preceding shear is $(S\sigma_p/\sigma)E_2\otimes E_1$. In the normal equation its transpose acts on $\lambda\zeta_2/S$, and in the amplitude equation the shear acts on $\alpha_1/S$. Both resulting coefficients are $-\sigma_p/\sigma$ in the respective scaled equations. The opposite placement of the factors $S^{-1}$ in Equation (2.3) retains both transfers.

r2a1.wave.frozen-couplings|TorusEuler.Mo.annotation: The positivity assumptions are on the two launch entries, not on every entry of $B$. Together with the nonzero preceding pair they give $r,S,\varepsilon>0$. Subsequent values of $B_{12},B_{32}$ are controlled by the relative variations in Equation (2.6), and need not be constant.

additive.time-scales|TorusEuler.MovingWa.annotation: The quantity $S=\sigma/r=r/(2\nu)$ measures the loss in recovering a general physical amplitude from the scaled plane coordinates. It is determined by the preceding wave, not by the launch frequency $\lambda$ of the present wave. In Section 7 the inherited bounds on $\sigma$ and $\nu$ give $CS\le C\lambda_{j-1}^{1/8}L_j$, a parent-scale cost in the transverse inverse.

r2a1.wave.reference-angle|TorusEuler.Pap.annotation: The choice $0\le\varphi<\pi/2$ gives $\cos\varphi>0$ on every finite interval. More quantitatively $\cos\varphi\ge T^{-2}$ on $[0,T]$ under $\varepsilon\le1$ and $T\ge2$. The same lower bound controls division by $\cos\varphi$ in Equation (2.15) and converts the additive error in the third coupling into an error relative to its small reference value.

r2a1.wave.constant-model-strength|TorusE.annotation: The model sets $B_{33}=0$ for the entire interval. By Equation (2.2), $(\log\sigma_p)'=0$ in either clock, so the ratio $\sigma_p/\sigma$ is identically one. This is the coefficient of the leading shear term after rescaling; the general case must control its drift instead.

r2a1.wave.model-vector-equations|TorusEu.annotation: Put $\mu=1/(2S^2)$. The last two rows preserve $\zeta_3^2+\mu\zeta_2^2=1$; also $\zeta_1+(1+\mu)\zeta_3/(\varepsilon\mu)$ is constant. The initial data therefore give $\zeta_3=\cos(\varepsilon\sqrt\mu\,\tau)$, $\zeta_2=-\sin(\varepsilon\sqrt\mu\,\tau)/\sqrt\mu$ and $\zeta_1=(1+\mu)(1-\zeta_3)/(\varepsilon\mu)$. Expanding the cosine at fixed $\tau$ gives the quadratic first component in Equation (2.4).

r2a1.wave.model-amplitude-equations|Toru.annotation:
In physical coordinates the three terms in $k\cdot M\mathbf a$ are $
u k_1a_2$, $\sigma k_2a_1$ and $\eta k_3a_2$. On inserting Equation (2.3) these become $
u\lambda\zeta_1\alpha_2$, $2
u\lambda\zeta_2\alpha_1$ and $\eta\lambda\zeta_3\alpha_2$. Using $|k|^2=\lambda^2m$ gives the displayed $\Pi=\lambda Sp_{m w}/r$.

r2a1.wave.reference-system|TorusEuler.Pa.annotation: Write $s=\cos\varphi$. The trace of the reference matrix is $2(\log s)'$, so the determinant of two solutions is proportional to $s^2$. Taking the columns to be $(-Ya_{\rm ref},a_{\rm ref})$ and $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$ gives the determinant $-a_{\rm ref}(\alpha_1+Y\alpha_2)$. This is the combination used in Equation (2.15) to measure departure from the reference direction, rather than absolute amplitude error.

The algebraic forms $c=(1-\varepsilon x)/(1+x^2)$ and $d=2\varepsilon\tau x/(1+x^2)$ are useful even at large $x$: their denominator is the squared reference wave-number factor, not an additional approximation. With $x=\tan\varphi$ they become the two trigonometric coefficients in Equation (2.5).

additive.finite-smallness|TorusEuler.Pap.annotation: The tolerance used in the coupling calculation is smaller than a fixed absolute error: the second coupling itself may be of order $T^{-2}\nu$. If a preceding estimate is $CT^p\delta$, then Equation (2.7) bounds it by $(C/C_0)\varepsilon T^{p-C_0}$. Taking $C_0\ge p+2$ and $C_0\ge8C$ gives the later tolerance $\varepsilon T^{-2}/8$. This is why the exponent in (2.7) is left sufficiently large.

The first inequality makes the reference ratio small; the second imposes the accuracy of the finite-shear comparison. In particular the model with constant moving entries and $E_c=0$ still has $\delta\ge\nu/r=1/(2S)>0$. Thus even the exact finite-shear model must have $S\ge C_0T^{C_0}/(2\varepsilon)$ to meet Equation (2.7). The reference limit, where $S^{-1}=0$, is not itself a finite physical wave.

r2a1.wave.strong-shear-bounds|TorusEuler.annotation: At activation $B_{12}=\nu$, so the third term of Equation (2.6) is at least $\nu/r=1/(2S)$. Consequently $S^{-1}\le2\delta$ and, since $\delta\le1/4$, $S^{-2}\le4\delta^2\le\delta$. Strong shear is therefore a consequence of the comparison hypotheses, not another assumption.

r2a1.wave.vector-comparison|TorusEuler.P.annotation: The second bound in Equation (2.10) is the one used in Proposition 2.8: at a late crossing, $\eta_+/\nu_+=\varepsilon_+$ is comparable to $\cos\varphi$, so $|k|\asymp\lambda/\varepsilon_+$. The amplitude comparison is still needed to control $|\mathbf a|$. Bounds on the two quantities separately explain why a very small coupling ratio can be selected after the velocity amplitude has already decreased.

r2a1.wave.safe-coordinates|TorusEuler.Mo.annotation: In particular $\zeta_3\ge1/2$ has a use beyond keeping the amplitude chart regular. The preceding vorticity points along $E_3$, while the vorticity of the new wave is perpendicular to $k$. In Section 8 the projection along $k/|k|$ eliminates the latter contribution and retains at least $\sigma_p/(2\sqrt m)$ of the preceding vorticity. Since $\sqrt m\le3T^2$ here, the retained projection costs only a polynomial in the normalized interval length.

r2a1.wave.strength-bound|TorusEuler.Pape.annotation: The drift estimate is not an additional comparison of the new amplitude. It controls the coefficient $\sigma_p/\sigma$ that multiplies $q$ in the new coupling calculation Equation (2.20). It also shows that a strong preceding shear does not disappear during the present wave's amplification interval: $\sigma_p\ge e^{-T\delta}\sigma$. Section 8 uses this same logarithmic strength equation to estimate the preceding vorticity between activations.

r2a1.wave.scaled-error-matrix|TorusEuler.annotation: The extra gradient changes the normal coefficient by $-PE_c^TP^{-1}/r$, where $P=\operatorname{diag}(1,S,1)$ acts in the preceding frame. Its norm is at most $(S/r)|E_c|=|E_c|/(2\nu)$ because $\|P^{-1}\|=1$. The factor $S$ is paid once, explaining the normalization of $E_c$ in Equation (2.6).

r2a1.wave.polynomial-vector-error|TorusE.annotation: The first variation-of-constants estimate has a residual involving the unknown actual vector $\zeta$, not only the reference vector. Writing $\zeta=\zeta_0+(\zeta-\zeta_0)$ produces a term $CT^C\delta\sup|\zeta-\zeta_0|$ on the right; Equation (2.7) permits moving it to the left. This closes the normal estimate before any division by $\zeta_3$ in the amplitude equation.

r2a1.wave.reference-matrix-values|TorusE.annotation: In signed coordinates the reference matrix is $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}-d&c\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, with $c=(1-\varepsilon x)/(1+x^2)$ and $d=2\varepsilon\tau x/(1+x^2)$. Thus the boxed terms retain two distinct effects of pressure, the damping $-d$ and the change of driving from $1$ to $c$. Reversing the first coordinate gives Equation (2.5).

r2a1.amp.riccati-problem|TorusEuler.Pape.annotation: Where $\alpha_2>0$, eliminating $\alpha_1$ gives $\alpha_2''+\varepsilon\tau\sin2\varphi\,\alpha_2'=\cos^2\varphi(1-\varepsilon\tan\varphi)\alpha_2$. Dividing by $\alpha_2$ and using $\alpha_2''/\alpha_2=Y'+Y^2$ gives Equation (2.12). The scalar equation depends on the direction of the pair, not its overall normalization. The proof below constructs the slope globally before reconstructing a positive second component.

r2a1.amp.reference-reconstruction|TorusE.annotation: Given the scalar solution $Y$, let $V=a_{\rm ref}$ and $U=YV$. Then $V'=U$ and $U'=(Y'+Y^2)V=cV-dU$, with $c$ the driving and $d$ the damping coefficient in Equation (2.5). The quadratic term has canceled, so this is the signed linear system. The reconstruction uses the Riccati equation; the additional condition $Y(0)=1$ selects the reference initial pair.

r2a1.amp.reference-ansatz|TorusEuler.Pap.annotation: The ansatz can also be read as a change of dependent variable and clock. With $s=\cos\varphi$, put $a_{\rm ref}=\sqrt{s}\,W(\theta)$, $\theta'=s$, $\theta(0)=0$. Since $Y=(\log a_{\rm ref})'$, Equation (2.13) gives $W_\theta/W=1+e$. The correction equation is equivalent to $W_{\theta\theta}=(1+\varepsilon\sin\varphi\cos\varphi/2)W$, with $W(0)=W_\theta(0)=1$. The coefficient lies between one and $1+\varepsilon/4$; the square-root factor accounts for the geometric loss as the normal turns.

At the peak the ansatz gives $\varepsilon\tau_m=2(1+e(\tau_m))/\sin\varphi(\tau_m)$. Since $\cos\varphi(\tau_m)\le\varepsilon/2$ and $e\le\varepsilon/8$, this is $2+O(\varepsilon)$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. After the peak the integral remaining in Equation (2.14) is bounded, so the amplitude quotient is comparable to the square root of the cosine quotient. The reference strength instead contains the inverse square root, because the wave number is $\lambda/\cos\varphi$.

r2a1.amp.reference-amplitude-formula|Tor.annotation: The two factors in Equation (2.14) have opposite effects on the amplitude: the exponential grows and the square root of the cosine decreases. For the reference shear, however, multiplication by $|k|=\lambda/\cos\varphi$ changes the latter factor into $(\cos\varphi)^{-1/2}$. Both factors then grow. It is the amplitude, not the shear, that has a maximum at $\tau_m$.

r2a1.amp.unique-zero|TorusEuler.Paper.St.annotation: At the zero of $Y$, Equation (2.13) gives $\varepsilon\tau_m=2(1+e(\tau_m))/\sin\varphi(\tau_m)$. The stated bracket implies $\cos\varphi(\tau_m)=O(\varepsilon)$, so in fact $\varepsilon\tau_m=2+O(\varepsilon)$ as $\varepsilon\to0$. The peak occurs with the normal nearly parallel to $E_1$, long after it has reached angle $\pi/4$ at $\sqrt{2/\varepsilon}$.

r2a1.amp.unique-zero|TorusEuler.Paper.le.annotation: At any zero, Equation (2.12) reduces to $Y'=s^2(1-(\varepsilon\tau)^2/2)$, with $s=\cos\varphi$. The ansatz first rules out zeros for $\varepsilon\tau\le2$. All remaining zeros have negative derivative; once the first is crossed, the function cannot return to zero from below. The opposite signs at $2/\varepsilon$ and $3/\varepsilon$ give existence.

r2a1.amp.reference-signs-maximum|TorusEu.annotation: The maximum in this lemma is that of the second scaled component of the reference solution. Later, Equation (2.18) compares the actual physical length with this component pointwise. Taking maxima preserves the two multiplicative inequalities, provided the comparison interval contains $\tau_m$; it does not locate the maximizing time of the physical length.

For the reference strength, the logarithmic derivative is $Y-(\log\cos\varphi)'=(1+e)\cos\varphi-\tfrac12(\log\cos\varphi)'>0$. In particular the decrease in amplitude after $\tau_m$ is more than offset by the increase in wave number. Later we will use the finite-shear comparison to estimate the actual strength at a crossing; monotonicity of the actual strength is not required. (The crossing-strength estimate is Equation (2.23).)

r2a1.amp.reference-gain|TorusEuler.Paper.annotation: The gain is a ratio of amplitudes, so one can use it in reverse. Given a desired maximum $A=\lambda^{-3/4}$ on the comparison slab, solve with the growing launch direction and multiply by $A/\max|\mathbf a|$. The frame and the crossing equation are unchanged. It is the resulting small initial amplitude, rather than an arbitrarily large final velocity, that is needed in Section 6.2.

r2a1.amp.angle-and-clock-derivatives|Tor.annotation: Writing $s=\cos\varphi$ and $x=\tan\varphi$, we have $s'/s=-xx'/(1+x^2)=-\varepsilon\tau\sin\varphi\cos\varphi$. Thus the coefficient of $Y$ in Equation (2.12) is $2s'/s$, and the correction in Equation (2.13) is $s'/(2s)$. The latter is the logarithmic derivative of the square-root prefactor in Equation (2.14).

r2a1.amp.ansatz-proof|TorusEuler.Referen.annotation: Another way to obtain the ansatz is to set $s=\cos\varphi$, $d\xi=s\,d\tau$ and $a_{\rm ref}=\sqrt{s}\,f(\xi)$. Then $Y/s-s'/(2s^2)=f_\xi/f$. In the scalar second-order equation obtained from Equation (2.5), this substitution eliminates the first derivative of $f$. The ansatz sets its logarithmic derivative equal to $1+e$.

r2a1.amp.integrated-ansatz|TorusEuler.Re.annotation: Between times $a$ and $b$, the integral in Equation (2.14) is replaced by its increment $\int_a^b(1+e)\cos\varphi$. The prefactor is replaced by $\sqrt{\cos\varphi(b)/\cos\varphi(a)}$. Choosing $a=\tau_m$ will remove the entire gain accumulated before the peak from the estimate for the retained amplitude.

r2a1.amp.global-deviation|TorusEuler.Pap.annotation: Solve the equation for $e$ first and define $Y$ by Equation (2.13). Then $a_{\rm ref}=\exp(\int_0^\tau Y)$ is positive, and direct substitution shows that $(-Ya_{\rm ref},a_{\rm ref})$ solves Equation (2.5) with the required data. This order avoids assuming that the second component of the reference solution never vanishes in order to derive a global equation for its quotient.

r2a1.amp.upper-rate|TorusEuler.Reference.annotation: To bound the positive part of $Y$, the equation at $Y\ge1$ gives $Y'\le1-Y^2\le0$. On the negative side Equation (2.13) gives $Y\ge-\min\{\varepsilon\tau/4,1/\tau\}\ge-\sqrt\varepsilon/2$. The paper needs only the resulting uniform bound $|Y|\le1$, which will also bound the entries of the coordinate change after the peak.

r2a1.amp.positive-before-turn|TorusEuler.annotation: The sign of the driving coefficient and the sign of $Y$ need not change at the same time: at $\tau=\sqrt2/\varepsilon$, the first term of Equation (2.12) vanishes but $Y>0$. By then the remaining effective growth time $\int_{\sqrt2/\varepsilon}^{\infty}\cos\varphi\,d\tau$ is at most $\sqrt2$. The large exponential gain has already occurred; the balance of this remaining gain with the decreasing cosine determines the peak.

r2a1.amp.normalized-l-decay|TorusEuler.R.annotation: Liouville gives $a_{\rm ref}^2l\cos\varphi$ proportional to $\cos^2\varphi$. On substituting Equation (2.14), this says that $(a_{\rm ref}/\sqrt{\cos\varphi})^2l$ is constant. In the effective time $d\xi=\cos\varphi\,d\tau$, this is the constant Wronskian of $f=a_{\rm ref}/\sqrt{\cos\varphi}$ and $\alpha_2/\sqrt{\cos\varphi}$. In particular $l$ decays like the inverse square of the growing factor $f$.

r2a1.amp.positive-second-amplitude|Torus.annotation: The change Equation (2.15) is available before any positivity of $\alpha_2$ has been proved. The estimate for $(h,l)$ can therefore be obtained on the whole slab without stopping at a hypothetical first zero of $\alpha_2$. Only afterward do we use $h\ge1/2$ to divide by $\alpha_2$.

r2a1.amp.amplitude-comparison|TorusEuler.annotation: The two estimates concern different parts of the reconstruction. From Equation (2.15), $q+Y=-l\cos\varphi/h$, which measures the error in the direction. From transversality, $z=-(\zeta_1q+\zeta_2)/\zeta_3$, so the length correction is $|\mathbf a|/\alpha_2=(1+S^{-2}(q^2+z^2))^{1/2}$. Both estimates follow once the normalized state is close to $(1,0)$.

r2a1.amp.log-amplitude-comparison|TorusE.annotation: Exponentiating Equation (2.18) gives a two-sided multiplicative comparison with the reference amplitude at every time. Applied at two times, this gives an error factor between $e^{-2\varepsilon}$ and $e^{2\varepsilon}$ in the ratio of their amplitudes, regardless of whether the reference amplitude is increasing or decreasing between them.

r2a1.amp.onto-transverse-transport|Torus.annotation: In Section 5 the same estimate is needed for every initial vector and for sources that need not lie in the growing direction. At a label $a$, the map $D_aX$ identifies the fixed plane $k_*^\perp$ with the moving plane $\kappa^\perp$. In these coordinates the origin estimate gives a propagator bounded by $\mathsf D^3\gamma(t)/\gamma(t')$. The generator at nearby labels is then compared with the one at zero by variation of constants; the amplitude weights cancel in the integral.

r2a1.amp.transport-bound|TorusEuler.Pape.annotation: For example, in physical time a transverse forcing $g$ with zero initial data gives $|\mathbf b(t)|\le CS\gamma(t)\int_{t_0}^t |g(t')|/\gamma(t')\,dt'$. There is no extra gain from integrating a forcing already proportional to $\gamma$. If a source is originally given in normalized time it must first be converted to physical time using $d\tau=r\,dt$. The hierarchy in Section 5 uses physical-time sources.

r2a1.amp.comparison-matrices|TorusEuler..annotation: The determinant of $R$ is $1/\cos\varphi$; its inverse has bounded entries. The poorly scaled direction is the excess of $-\beta_1$ over $Y\beta_2$, whose natural unit in Equation (2.15) is $a_{\rm ref}\cos\varphi$. Thus the factor in the condition number comes from measuring the direction on a finer scale, not from a small reference amplitude.

r2a1.amp.comparison-conjugation|TorusEul.annotation: Put $P=R/a_{\rm ref}$ and let $N_0$ be the reference matrix. The coefficient in the new coordinates is $P'P^{-1}+PN_0P^{-1}+P\mathcal EP^{-1}$. The first two terms are exactly the matrix in Equation (2.16); in the last term the scalar $a_{\rm ref}$ cancels. Hence even the perturbation is multiplied only by the condition number of $R$, which is polynomial in $T$.

r2a1.amp.positive-ratio-identity|TorusEu.annotation: The identity actually gives $|\alpha_1/\alpha_2+Y|=\cos\varphi\,|l/h|$. In particular the scaled direction error is bounded by $CT^C\delta\cos\varphi$, even when the reference first component passes through zero. This stronger form follows from Equation (2.15); the linked Lean quotient estimate drops the cosine factor. The finer scale is natural for the small successor turning coupling.

r2a1.amp.physical-propagator-conclusion|.annotation: After peak normalization, $\gamma(t)=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a(t)|$ is positive and has maximum one. For a parent scale $\mathsf D\ge CS$, the inequality becomes $|\mathbf b(t)|/\gamma(t)\le\mathsf D|\mathbf b(t')|/\gamma(t')$, the first condition in Equation (5.5). The other condition, $\nu_+\ge\mathsf D^{-1}$, follows from Lemma 2.7 if $\mathsf D\ge2/(\nu\varepsilon)$. The same scale controls propagation and the pressure sign.

c8-pressure-coupling-identity|TorusEuler.annotation: For the affine profile the central pressure Hessian is $-2\nu_+\sigma_+ E_{1,+}\otimes E_{1,+}$, where $\sigma_+=|\mathbf a||k|$. When $\nu_+>0$, as established below, its nonzero eigenvalue is negative. In the localized profile it is the lower bound $F_h'\ge-Ch$ that controls positive curvature of this leading tensor. The large negative central curvature is allowed by the upper quadratic-form bound used for the endpoint inverse in Section 4; the slow derivatives and correction pressures must still be estimated.

r2a1.amp.coupling-hypotheses|TorusEuler..annotation: For the next comparison $M$ becomes the older gradient, and $\mathbf a\otimes k$ becomes the preceding shear. Since $(\mathbf a\otimes k)E_{2,+}=0$, that shear changes the strength without changing either of the pairings defining $\nu_+,\eta_+$. The completed periodic parent has an additional central gradient error $E_{c,+}$ from Theorem 7.1 (T4). It belongs in the error term of the next comparison, not in the pair whose ratio is prescribed exactly.

r2a1.amp.coupling-definitions|TorusEuler.annotation: Here $M$ is the gradient over which the current wave is evolved. Thus $\nu_+$ both determines its pressure coefficient and is the older-gradient entry to be frozen when the successor is launched. The corrected gradient at that launch also contains the new rank-one shear and an error. The shear annihilates $E_{2,+}$; the error is controlled separately by Equation (2.6) in the next step.

lem-2-5-positive-coupling|TorusEuler.Pap.annotation: For $\varepsilon\tan\varphi\le1$, $Y>0$ gives a reference lower bound $\varepsilon$ for $\nu_+/\nu$. In the complementary range the reference value is $1+O(\varepsilon^2)$, hence also at least $\varepsilon$ when Equation (2.7) holds with sufficiently large $C_0$. The additive comparison error is smaller than this common margin.

lem-2-5-late-time|TorusEuler.Paper.State.annotation: The condition $\varepsilon\tan\varphi\ge1$ is equivalent to $\tau\ge\sqrt2/\varepsilon$, the time when the driving coefficient in Equation (2.5) changes sign. It precedes the amplitude maximum. In particular the entire bracket used in Proposition 2.8 will be in the range of Equation (2.19), even though the start of that bracket is chosen using the amplitude rather than the couplings.

r2a1.amp.coupling-ratio-coordinates|Toru.annotation: At the reference normal, $z=-xq+\varepsilon\tau$ with $x=\tan\varphi$. Substituting $q=-Y$ from Equation (2.13) yields $z_0=(1+e)\sin\varphi+\tfrac12\varepsilon\tau(1+\cos^2\varphi)$. This component can grow after the amplitude peaks. In comparing $z$ at a fixed reference normal, however, the direction error $q+Y=-\cos\varphi\,l/h$ is multiplied by $x$, giving only $\sin\varphi\,l/h$ in $z-z_0$.

r2a1.amp.strain-coupling-error|TorusEule.annotation: For unit vectors the contribution of $E_c$ to either normalized entry is at most $\|E_c\|/\nu$. In Equation (2.6) this is part of $\delta$. Lean works with the gradient divided by $r$ and multiplies the bound by $2S=r/\nu$ to convert it back to the old-coupling scale.

r2a1.amp.coupling-cancellation|TorusEule.annotation: With $s=\cos\varphi$ and $u=\varepsilon\tau\sin\varphi/2$, the second expression divided by $s$ can be written as $2(Y/s+u)^2-1+\varepsilon\tan\varphi-2u^2$. The first square is $2(1+e)^2$ by Equation (2.13). The last two terms must be combined before estimating them; bounding them separately loses the small cosine scale.

r2a1.amp.positive-actual-coupling|TorusE.annotation: The lower bound is relative to the central lengths: with $\mathsf D\ge2/(\nu\varepsilon)$ it gives $k\cdot M\mathbf a\ge\mathsf D^{-1}|k||\mathbf a|$. In Section 5.4, relative changes of size $d$ in $k$ and $\mathbf a$ and an absolute change of size $d$ in $M$ change this contraction by at most $4\mathsf D d|k||\mathbf a|$ (central lengths on the right). Thus $d\le(8\mathsf D^2)^{-1}$ suffices for positivity on the envelope, without needing an exponentially small radius to match the launch amplitude.

r2a1.amp.actual-relative-couplings|Torus.annotation: For the iteration the first inequality of Equation (2.19) is needed with its actual error $\varepsilon$, since successive changes of $\nu$ must be summable. For locating a crossing the second inequality need only give comparability with the cosine. It is not necessary to control the derivative or monotonicity of the physical quotient.

lem-2-6-inherited-assumptions|TorusEuler.annotation: Write $\mu=\lambda_{j-1}$ in Section 7. The full comparison interval is $[t_j,S_j]$, of length $2\tau_j=2\mu^{-1/8}L_{j+1}^3$. Its prescribed crossing bracket ends at normalized time $2L_jL_{j+1}$, since $\varepsilon= L_j^{-2}$ and $\varepsilon_+=L_{j+1}^{-2}$. The lower bound $r_j\gtrsim\mu^{1/8}$ places this endpoint before $t_j+\tau_j$; the second half of the interval leaves room for the successor's construction.

lem-2-6-crossing-existence|TorusEuler.Pa.annotation: The peak time serves two purposes. Since $\tau_m\ge2/\varepsilon>\sqrt2/\varepsilon$, the late comparison (2.19) holds throughout the crossing bracket. Also the reference amplitude has attained its maximum by the left endpoint, so its subsequent decay can be estimated by integrating Equation (2.14) from $\tau_m$. Neither argument identifies the maximizing time of the actual amplitude.

r2a1.amp.all-crossings-strength|TorusEul.annotation: Fix the entire comparison slab first, so that $A=\max_{[0,T]}|\mathbf a|$ is known before choosing a crossing. Positive rescaling multiplies $A$ and $\sigma_+$ by the same constant, preserves both unit directions and leaves the two couplings unchanged. It therefore preserves every crossing and the ratio in Equation (2.23), but changes the strength passed to the next wave.

lem-2-6-strength|TorusEuler.Paper.propos.annotation: Substituting $A=\lambda_j^{-3/4}$, $\varepsilon=L_j^{-2}$ and $\varepsilon_+=L_{j+1}^{-2}$ gives $\sigma_j\asymp\lambda_j^{1/4}L_jL_{j+1}$ at the crossing. The next growth rate is therefore $r_{j+1}\asymp\lambda_j^{1/8}\sqrt{L_jL_{j+1}}$. Both bounds on the strength are useful: in Section 7 the lower bound on the rate fits the next crossing into its short physical interval, while the upper bound controls the length of the normalized interval in Equation (2.7).

lem-2-6-early-gain|TorusEuler.Paper.Stat.annotation: The interval in Equation (2.24) is the time during which the cutoff varies, of physical length $1/r$. The estimate must hold throughout that interval, not merely at launch. The crossing used for the successor is later than $2/\varepsilon>1$, so the full rank-one shear is present throughout the successor's active interval as long as it lies inside the present slab.

lem-2-6-early-gain|TorusEuler.Paper.prop.annotation: For wave $j$, the choice $\varepsilon^{-1/2}=L_j=4\log\lambda_{j+1}$ gives $\gamma\le e^3\lambda_{j+1}^{-4}$ while the cutoff varies. Since $|\widetilde\chi'|\le Cr_j$, this controls $\|\widetilde\chi'\gamma\|_\infty$, the activation factor in Equation (5.48), by $Ce^3r_j\lambda_{j+1}^{-4}$. The expansion depth $P=6K_{j+1}$ gives the other factor $\lambda_j^{-2P/3}=\lambda_{j+1}^{-4}$. Both errors can then pay the frequency and parent losses in the physical residual estimate.

ret-proof-turning-bracket|TorusEuler.Ref.annotation: The entire interval $[\tau_m,T]$ lies in the range $\varepsilon\tan\varphi\ge1$ because $\tau_m\ge2/\varepsilon>\sqrt2/\varepsilon$. The estimates of Equation (2.19) can thus be used not only at the two endpoints but at any crossing found in this late interval.

r2a1.amp.late-clock-coupling-bounds|Toru.annotation: For $x=\tan\varphi\ge1$, the estimate $\sqrt{1+x^2}\le2x$ gives $\cos\varphi\ge1/(2x)$. Since $x(\tau_m)\le9/(2\varepsilon)$, Equation (2.19) yields $\rho(\tau_m)\ge\varepsilon/18$, where $\rho=\eta_+/\nu_+$. This strict margin above $\varepsilon_+\le\varepsilon/32$ avoids any need to estimate the ratio at the actual amplitude maximum.

r2a1.amp.crossing-upper-endpoint|TorusEu.annotation: At $H=2/\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}$ the reference tangent is $2/\varepsilon_+$, hence $\cos\varphi(H)\le\varepsilon_+/2$. The error factor in Equation (2.19) allows the actual ratio to exceed the cosine by as much as $3/2$. The extra factor in the choice of $H$ leaves the strict bound $3\varepsilon_+/4$.

r2a1.amp.crossing-clock-scale|TorusEuler.annotation: At any late crossing the tangent bounds give $1/\sqrt{2\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}\le\tau\le\sqrt{3/(\varepsilon\varepsilon_+)}$. Thus the elapsed physical time is comparable to $1/(r\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+})$, no matter which crossing in the bracket is chosen. In the induction the upper bound fits the next activation into the present slab, and a lower bound on the elapsed time is also used in Section 8 for the vorticity integral.

r2a1.amp.exponential-amplitude-compariso.annotation: From Equation (2.18), exponentiation of the bound on the logarithm gives $e^{-\varepsilon}a_{\rm ref}\le|\mathbf a|\le e^\varepsilon a_{\rm ref}$. The linked implication requires positive amplitudes; Lemma 2.6 ensures this and the bound at every time of the slab.

r2a1.amp.ratio-to-actual-maximum|TorusEu.annotation: Put $A=\max_{[0,T]}|\mathbf a|$ and $A_m=a_{\rm ref}(\tau_m)$. The lower estimate in Equation (2.18) at $\tau_m$ gives $A\ge e^{-\varepsilon}A_m$, and the upper estimate at every point of the slab gives $A\le e^\varepsilon A_m$. Dividing the pointwise amplitude estimates by these opposite bounds gives an error factor at most $e^{2\varepsilon}$ in the ratios to the maxima. No comparison of the maximizing times is needed.

r2a1.amp.wave-number-comparison|TorusEul.annotation: Equation (2.10) gives $|k|\asymp\lambda/\cos\varphi$; the linked late estimate writes the same scale as $\lambda\tan\varphi$. Notice also that the $E_3$ component of $k/\lambda$ remains bounded below by $1/2$. In Section 8, projecting the vorticity onto $k/|k|$ therefore retains a component comparable to $\cos\varphi$ of the preceding wave's vorticity, while eliminating the new wave's leading curl.

r2a1.amp.late-strength-comparison|TorusE.annotation: In the late interval the strength and the turning ratio obey $\varepsilon(\eta_+/\nu_+)\,[|\mathbf a||k|/(\lambda A)]^2\asymp1$, with $A=\max_{[0,T]}|\mathbf a|$. This follows by multiplying the squared strength bound, of order $1/(\varepsilon\cos\varphi)$, by the ratio bound in Equation (2.19). Specifying the next ratio therefore fixes the scale of the available strength, independently of which late crossing is selected.

r2a1.amp.turning-clock-scale|TorusEuler..annotation: The tangent at the peak is of order $1/\varepsilon$, so the cosine there is of order $\varepsilon$. More precisely, the zero relation in Equation (2.13) yields $\varepsilon\tau_m=2+O(\varepsilon)$ and hence $\cos\varphi(\tau_m)=(\varepsilon/2)(1+O(\varepsilon))$. It is this small peak cosine, not the launch value one, that normalizes the retained amplitude.

ret-proof-early-gain-conclusion|TorusEul.annotation: The early bound in Equation (2.24) compares with the maximum over the full slab. Indeed $Y\le1$ gives $a_{\rm ref}\le e$ in the first unit of time, while the reference maximum is at least $\exp(\varepsilon^{-1/2}-1)$. The two uses of Equation (2.18) add at most $2\varepsilon\le1$ to the logarithm of their ratio. This accounts for the constant three in the exponent.

localized.seed-equation|TorusEuler.affin.annotation: Write the correction to $-M\mathbf a$ as $p_{\rm w}\kappa$. Differentiating $\kappa\cdot\mathbf a$ gives $-2\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a+p_{\rm w}|\kappa|^2$. There are two equal terms because the normal itself moves by $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$. Canceling them determines the pressure coefficient in Equation (3.3).

localized.leading-profile-pressure|Torus.annotation: The phase derivative of $\mathsf p[A_1]$ is $-p_{\rm w}gF_0$, so its fast gradient cancels the part of the amplitude acceleration along $\kappa$. Its slow gradient is $-P_0\mathbf d(p_{\rm w}g)$; it need not be zero when the amplitude or envelope varies between particles. This term enters the next level in Equation (5.25).

localized.completion-definition|TorusEul.annotation: The slow curl $C[V]$ is obtained by differentiating $Q[V]$ at fixed $s$. In particular it is not the curl of the graph-evaluated potential: that curl also contains the prescribed velocity $V$. Since $Q[V]$ carries $|\kappa|^{-1}$, the slow correction in Equation (5.31) costs one label derivative but no factor $|\kappa|/h$.

localized.completed-velocity-longitudina.annotation: For the leading wave, Equation (3.6) reads $\kappa\cdot C[A_1]=-P_0(s)\,\mathbf d\cdot(g\mathbf a)$. Thus the phase velocity introduced by the completion can be computed from the slow divergence of the envelope and seed. In particular the mean of a fast interaction satisfies $\langle(\kappa\cdot C[V])\partial_s Y\rangle_s=\langle(\mathbf d\cdot V)Y\rangle_s$ by integration by parts; this is used at Equation (5.42).

Apply the full slow-fast divergence to the completed field. The slow curl has zero slow divergence, and the transverse $V$ has zero fast divergence. Thus the remaining two terms give $\partial_s(\kappa\cdot C[V])=-\mathbf d\cdot V$. This is a derivative identity; obtaining Equation (3.6) without an additive function of the labels uses the zero phase mean of $C[V]$.

localized.longitudinal-derivative|TorusE.annotation: The derivative on $Y$ in a product $(\kappa\cdot C[V])\partial_sY$ can be moved to $\kappa\cdot C[V]$ inside a phase average. Its derivative is $-\mathbf d\cdot V$, so the mean is $\langle(\mathbf d\cdot V)Y\rangle_s$. The fast interaction need not be small pointwise for this reduction to hold; it is the averaged interaction that loses the fast derivative in Equation (5.42).

localized.leading-potential|TorusEuler.w.annotation: In this formula $\mathbf a$ and $\kappa$ are orthogonal, so $|Q[A_1]|=|gP_0|\,|\mathbf a|/|\kappa|$. Unlike the leading velocity, the potential uses $P_0$ and need not vanish at $s=0$. Its slow curl is therefore not required to have zero central gradient, a contribution that is estimated separately in Equation (5.50).

localized.completion-derivative-cost|Tor.annotation: In differentiating $Q[V]$, each $\mathbf d_j$ acts on $\partial_s^{-1}V$ or on the coefficient $\kappa/|\kappa|^2$. The latter varies on the parent scale: $\kappa=(D_aX)^{-T}k_*$. This is why the coefficient estimates in Equation (5.8) and a single additional label derivative of $V$ suffice for the inverse-frequency estimate (5.31).

localized.switched-profiles|TorusEuler.L.annotation: The phase pressure must be switched by the same factor as the leading velocity. In Equation (3.4), $V_{1,t}+MV_1+\kappa\partial_s\mathsf p_1=\widetilde\chi\,0+\widetilde\chi' A_1$. When the slow curl is included the extra switching term is $\widetilde\chi'(A_1+C[A_1])$, as in Equation (3.8).

localized.flat-zero-extension|TorusEuler.annotation: This auxiliary flat-multiplier lemma gives smooth zero extension for a smooth seed on the future side of $t_0$ and a globally smooth flat cutoff. The slab version is used directly for Equation (3.7); in both cases flatness removes any boundary term from differentiating the extension.

localized.affine-pressure-control|TorusE.annotation: The affine coefficient and normal do not depend on space, so differentiating $-p_{\rm w}P_h(k\cdot x)$ twice leaves just $-p_{\rm w}F_h'(k\cdot x)k\otimes k$. The localized version also differentiates the coefficient and transported normal, as displayed in Equation (5.51).

localized.lemma31.parity-periodicity-pri.annotation: The primitive of an odd periodic $F_h$ with zero mean is even when normalized by its mean. In particular $P_h'(0)=0$, but $P_h(0)$ need not be zero. At the origin this distinction eliminates the mixed terms in Equation (5.51), without eliminating the slow coefficient Hessian multiplied by $P_h(0)$.

sec4.select-initial|TorusEuler.PaperSmoo.annotation: This is a linear boundary-value problem even when the parent is not an exact Euler flow. The initial position determines $\xi(0)=0$, while Equation (1.5) gives $\xi_t(0)=b(0)$. We solve for the latter so that $\xi(T)=0$. The uniqueness statement compares solutions with the same force and parent on the same entire slab.

sec4.coefficients|TorusEuler.endpointHes.annotation: Differentiating $F_t=MF$ gives $F_{tt}=(M_t+M^2)F$, with $F=D_aX$. Hence $F_{tt}+H^\# F=0$. In particular each column of $F$ satisfies the homogeneous vector ODE at a fixed label, though it does not have the two zero endpoint traces of an admissible displacement. The coefficient $H^\#$ depends only on the parent flow, and Equation (4.3) expresses it in terms of the pressure and residual.

sec4.coefficients|TorusEuler.kineticForm.annotation: Since $Kv\cdot v=|D_aXv|^2=|B|^2$, $K$ measures the physical velocity correction in label coordinates. The energy in Equation (1.8) instead involves $|\xi_t|^2=|M\xi+B|^2$. The cross term in this last square is accounted for by the vorticity form and the boundary derivative in Equation (4.7).

sec4.coefficients|TorusEuler.Paper.meanH.annotation: The identity $H^\#=-F_{tt}F^{-1}$ makes independence of the chosen $p$ in Equation (4.3) transparent. If $p$ is changed by a smooth function $r$, then $R$ changes by $\nabla r$, leaving $D^2p-\nabla R$ unchanged. For the later truncated parent, the choice of pressure is made to render its residual divergence free.

sec4.coefficients|TorusEuler.Paper.meanV.annotation: Using $F_t=MF$ we have $\Omega=F_t^TF-F^TF_t$ and $\Omega_t=F^T(H^\#-(H^\#)^T)F$. For an exact Euler parent, the Hessian is symmetric, so $\Omega$ is constant in time (the pulled-back vorticity form). For an approximate parent, Equation (4.3) gives $H^\#-(H^\#)^T=((\nabla R)^T-\nabla R)\circ X$. The inverse allows the resulting time dependence of $\Omega$.

sec4.inverse-bound|TorusEuler.Paper.Stat.annotation: For the stationary shear of Section 1.1, or any constant multiple of it, $M$ is constant along each trajectory and $M^2=0$. Thus $H^\#=0$, whereas $F=I+tM$ and $F^{-1}=I-tM$ can be arbitrarily large as the shear is increased. The curvature hypothesis cannot replace the inverse-deformation bound, even for exact Euler parents.

sec4.flow-identities|TorusEuler.IsLabelF.annotation: The flow equation implies $\partial_tF(t,a)=M(t,a)F(t,a)$ and $F(0,a)=I$. In particular $F(t,a)F(s,a)^{-1}$ transports a homogeneous displacement from $s$ to $t$. This is the same fundamental matrix that weights the forcing $b\circ X$ in the solution of Equation (1.5).

sec4.residual|TorusEuler.momentumResidua.annotation:
With the pressure convention $\Delta p_U=-\operatorname{tr}((
abla U)^2)$ in Section 5.1, $\operatorname{div}R_U=0$ since $\operatorname{div}((U\cdot
abla)U)=\operatorname{tr}((
abla U)^2)$. Thus $R_U$ is the actual defect of the projected Euler equation. Its gradient enters Equation (4.3), whereas the field itself is canceled by the first mean source.

sec4.residual-gradient|TorusEuler.endpoi.annotation: The pressure condition in Theorem 7.1 is chosen so that Equation (4.3) can be used even after truncation. If the parent has frequencies at most $2\mathsf D$, then $R_U$ has frequencies at most $4\mathsf D$ and $\|\nabla R_U\|_\infty\le C\mathsf D\|R_U\|_\infty$. In the induction the parent velocity has frequencies at most $2\mu^5$ and the preceding residual has size $\lambda^{-3}$, giving $H^\#\le(2/N+C\mu^5\lambda^{-3})I\le I$.

sec4.first-variation-equation|TorusEuler.annotation: One can identify the label displacement directly by composing the perturbed flow with the inverse of the parent flow. At first order, $X^{-1}\circ X_\delta=\operatorname{Id}+\delta z+O(\delta^2)$. Thus $z=F^{-1}\xi$ and $Fz_t=b\circ X$ by Equations (1.5) and (4.4). Since the relative map preserves volume, $\operatorname{div}_a z=0$.

sec4.norm-equivalence|TorusEuler.integra.annotation: From Equation (4.4), $\|z_t\|_2\le D_-(\|\xi_t\|_2+\|M\|_\infty\|\xi\|_2)$. The terminal Poincaré inequality bounds $\|\xi\|_2$ by $(T/\sqrt2)\|\xi_t\|_2\le\|\xi_t\|_2$. Squaring gives Equation (4.6) for differentiable paths; the Sobolev version uses the same inequality almost everywhere.

sec4.norm-equivalence|TorusEuler.Paper.L.annotation: For an $L^2$ path $v$ with zero integral, take its absolutely continuous primitive $z$. Then $Fz$ has weak derivative $MFz+Fv$ by the Sobolev product rule. The same Poincaré and triangle inequalities give Equation (4.6) in this class. Thus the estimate can be used for a time-path solution of Appendix A, before recovering its continuous representative.

sec4.label-energy|TorusEuler.endpointL2E.annotation: The integral is the quadratic form of the integrated operator acting on $v=z_t$. With $Jv=z$, time integration by parts gives $\int_I J(\Omega v)\cdot v=-\int_I\Omega v\cdot z$, since $z$ vanishes at the endpoints. This is why the minus sign of the integral in Equation (4.9) produces a plus sign in the mixed energy here.

sec4.integrated-energy|TorusEuler.integr.annotation: The integrated boundary term is $-[\xi\cdot M\xi]_0^T$, which vanishes at both ends. To pass from smooth velocities to $L^2$ velocities of zero integral, subtract the time mean from each smooth approximant. Their primitives retain the two traces, and the operations $v\mapsto FJv$ and $v\mapsto MFJv+Fv$ are continuous in $L^2$. This gives Equation (4.7) without a classical time derivative of $v$.

sec4.hardy-hypothesis|TorusEuler.paper_m.annotation: The hypothesis is an upper bound on the symmetric part of $H^\#$, not on $\|M_t+M^2\|$. For instance a large negative eigenvalue does not reduce the lower bound in Equation (4.7). The construction in Section 3 exploits exactly this asymmetry: a large negative contribution to the pressure Hessian is compatible with a small upper bound.

sec4.hardy-hessian|TorusEuler.paper_mean.annotation: It is $\xi=Fz$ that appears in the potential term of Equation (4.7). Its end traces vanish, so $\int H^\#\xi\cdot\xi\le\int|\xi|^2\le(T^2/2)\int|\xi_t|^2$. Estimating $\xi$ instead via $\|F\|\|z\|$ would introduce an unnecessary parent-deformation factor into the curvature restriction.

sec4.hardy-coercive|TorusEuler.paper_mea.annotation: Writing $\mu=[2D_-^2(1+\|M\|_\infty)^2]^{-1}$, Equations (4.6) and (4.8) give $\langle (K-J\Omega)v,v\rangle_{L^2_t}\ge\mu\|v\|_{L^2_t}^2$ for $\int_Iv=0$. This is the path-space lower bound, independent of the spatial projection. It estimates the norm of an entire path; a separate spatial inversion will be needed to estimate its endpoint values.

sec4.integrated-equation|TorusEuler.Pape.annotation: For the parent at rest, $K=I$, $\Omega=0$ and Equation (4.9) reduces to $v+L=c+\nabla\phi$. Writing $\overline L$ for the time mean, we obtain $v=-\mathbb P(L-\overline L)$, $c=\mathbb P\overline L$, $\nabla\phi=(I-\mathbb P)L$. Here the zero time mean selects the initial correction, whereas the spatial projection selects the pressure gradient. The same distinction is used in Appendix A for nonconstant coefficients.

Given a displacement satisfying Equation (4.9), differentiate in time only to obtain $v=z_t$ in the closed solenoidal space. The two traces imply $z=Jv$ and $\int_Iv=0$. Projecting the original integrated equation, without differentiating its source, gives the velocity formulation in the linked declaration. This direction is useful for uniqueness of solutions expressed as displacements.

The pressure variable at this regularity is a continuous curve $G=\nabla_a\phi$ of periodic gradients, determined by Equation (4.9). No time derivative of the scalar potential is required. The other variables are a continuous solenoidal $v$, its primitive $z$ with two zero traces, and a time-independent solenoidal $c$. The pressure gradient and $c$ can both be recovered once $v$ is found.

sec4.constant-initial|TorusEuler.PaperMe.annotation: Evaluating Equation (4.9) at zero with $L(0)=0$ gives $v(0)=c+\nabla_a\phi(0)$. Both $v(0)$ and $c$ are solenoidal. A solenoidal periodic gradient is zero, so in fact $c=v(0)=b(0)$ and $\nabla_a\phi(0)=0$. The first equality is the linked lemma; the conclusion about the gradient follows from the same equation.

sec4.inverse-hypothesis|TorusEuler.Paper.annotation: The theorem estimates the response to the integrated datum $L$, for which time continuity is enough. It gives $z\in C^1_tC_a^{0,1/2}$ and a continuous pressure gradient in the integrated equation. To recover Equation (4.11) we need an additional time derivative of $v$ and of the gradient; these follow in the smooth-force clause below.

The velocity formulation and the displacement formulation give the same solution: $v=z_t$ is solenoidal with zero integral, and conversely $z=Jv$. Thus uniqueness of the projected velocity implies uniqueness of $z$ and, by the decomposition of Equation (4.9), of $c$ and the gradient. This argument needs no time derivative of $L$.

sec4.inverse-polynomial|TorusEuler.Paper.annotation: The inverse-deformation and strain bounds enter the reciprocal coercivity constants as $D_-^2$ and $2D_-^2(1+\|M\|_\infty)^2$. The spatial norms of $K$ and $\Omega$ then determine how small a neighborhood is needed for freezing coefficients in Lemma A.2. The Lean statement separates the supremum and first-derivative bounds for each coefficient. These are controlled by the norms in Equation (4.10).

The exponent in Equation (4.10) must be absolute for the use in Section 5.3. On the envelope scale $\ell_*$, the coefficient bound there gives $\ell_*^m(|K|_{m,1/2}+|\Omega|_{m,1/2})\le C_m/A$ for $m\ge1$. Each differentiated-coefficient term in the equation for $\partial_a^\beta v$ therefore loses a factor $A$ from the inverse and gains $A^{-1}$ from that bound. Induction gives $\|v\|_{[n],1/2}\le C_n A\|L\|_{[n],1/2}$, keeping the exponent of the parent size independent of $n$.

sec4.velocity-bound|TorusEuler.Paper.the.annotation: The mixed norm from Equation (A.8) is sufficient for the primitive: $\|J(\Omega v)(t)-J(\Omega v)(s)\|_{C_a^{0,1/2}}\le |t-s|^{1/2}\|\Omega v\|_{C_a^{0,1/2}(L_t^2)}$. This follows by applying Cauchy–Schwarz both to the values and to spatial increments. Thus the known right side of Equation (A.9) is continuous even before $v$ has been shown continuous in time.

sec4.smooth-displacement|TorusEuler.pape.annotation: The proof gains spatial regularity first, using Lemma A.2 at all derivative orders, then obtains $v\in C_tC_a^{k,1/2}$ for every $k$ by Equation (A.9). That equation expresses $v$ using the smooth coefficient inverse and a primitive of $\Omega v$, which now has a time derivative. Repeating the argument gives joint smoothness; it avoids differentiating the original $L^2$ time path.

sec4.smooth-displacement|TorusEuler.Pape.annotation: This link goes in the reverse direction from the smoothness assertion. Starting with a smooth correction, integrate its label momentum equation with $L=-Jg$ to get a solution of Equation (4.9). Consequently the uniqueness theorem for integrated data compares any two smooth solutions of the physical problem, including solutions obtained by a different construction.

sec4.normalized-pressure|TorusEuler.pape.annotation: The smooth field $G_q=g-\mathcal Dv-Kv_t$ has zero Leray projection. On the torus its Fourier coefficient at nonzero $n$ is parallel to $n$, and its zero coefficient is zero, so it is the gradient of a periodic potential. Requiring the potential's zero Fourier coefficient to vanish makes it unique. This is the instantaneous pressure in Equation (4.11), not the integrated pressure in Equation (4.9).

sec4.normalized-pressure|TorusEuler.Pape.annotation:
There are two pressure gradients: the integrated gradient $
abla_a\phi$ in Equation (4.9) and the instantaneous gradient $
abla_a\mathsf q$ in Equation (4.11). They satisfy $
abla_a\mathsf q=-\partial_t
abla_a\phi$ for smooth forces. The zero-mean convention for $\mathsf q$ concerns its spatial mean at each time, not its average over the interval.

For smooth data the gradient in Equation (4.9) is a smooth field, and $-\partial_t\nabla_a\phi=g-\mathcal Dv-Kv_t$. There is no need to choose and differentiate an unnormalized scalar $\phi$; the right side has zero Leray projection and directly determines a normalized periodic potential. This is how the proof supplies a smooth scalar pressure rather than only its gradient.

sec4.strong-label|TorusEuler.Paper.State.annotation:
Differentiate Equation (4.9): the left side becomes $Kv_t+K_tv-\Omega v-g$, while the derivative of $c$ is zero. Using $K_t-\Omega=\mathcal D$ and $
abla_a\mathsf q=-\partial_t
abla_a\phi$ gives $Kv_t+
abla_a\mathsf q=g-\mathcal Dv$. The negative primitive of the force is responsible for the positive $g$ on the right.

sec4.strong-label|TorusEuler.Paper.theor.annotation: On the solenoidal space, projection of Equation (4.11) gives $v_t=S(t)^{-1}\mathbb P(g-\mathcal Dv)$ with $S(t)=\mathbb P K(t)$. This is an evolution equation once $v(0)$ is known. Its initial value must come from Equation (4.9), since the evolution equation by itself imposes no zero-integral condition on $v$.

sec4.smooth-eulerian|TorusEuler.Paper.St.annotation: The formula $b=(Fv)\circ X^{-1}$ is the pushforward of the label velocity as a vector field. For the pressure, $q=\mathsf q\circ X^{-1}$ is ordinary scalar composition, hence $(\nabla_x q)\circ X=F^{-T}\nabla_a\mathsf q$. Using the same vector transformation for pressure would not give Equation (4.12).

sec4.eulerian-equation|TorusEuler.PaperS.annotation: Multiply Equation (4.11) by $F^{-T}$. The two left-hand terms become $Fv_t$ and $(\nabla_x q)\circ X$, and $F^{-T}\mathcal Dv=2F_tv$. Since $B=Fv$ and $MB=F_tv$, the resulting equation is $B_t+MB+(\nabla_xq)\circ X=f\circ X$. This is Equation (4.12) along the particle trajectories.

sec4.eulerian-equation|TorusEuler.Paper..annotation: Adding a periodic gradient $\nabla r$ to the force adds $r-\int r$ to the normalized pressure and leaves $b$ unchanged. Indeed the endpoint and divergence conditions are unchanged and the new pair satisfies Equation (4.12), so uniqueness identifies the velocity. Thus the mean inverse depends only on the solenoidal part of the physical source.

The mean solve in Equation (5.27) produces $B_p=b_p\circ X$. In Equation (5.28) it contributes $-(B_p\cdot\kappa)\partial_sV_1$ to the transverse source. Since $B_p$ and $\kappa$ are independent of $s$, this term has zero phase mean. The mean can therefore be found first, and only then inserted into the transverse equation; there is no additional mean unknown to solve for at that level.

sec4.endpoint-selection|TorusEuler.Paper.annotation: Averaging Equation (4.9) after spatial projection gives $c=\mathbb P[\overline{Kv}+\overline L-T^{-1}\int_0^T(T-s)\Omega(s)v(s)\,ds]$, where the bar denotes the time mean. For force data this field is $b(0)$. The formula displays the dependence on the whole interval, including the contribution of the skew term to the selected initial value.

sec4.fixed-time-inverse|TorusEuler.Paper.annotation: The fixed-time inverse supplies a continuous representative: $S(t)^{-1}-S(s)^{-1}=S(t)^{-1}(S(s)-S(t))S(s)^{-1}$, and the inverses are uniformly bounded. The right side of Equation (A.9) is continuous in the spatial norm, so the reconstructed $v$ is continuous. Testing its difference from the original time path at almost every time against that difference gives zero by ellipticity; hence its time integral is still zero.

r2.s34.rescale-endpoint|TorusEuler.Paper.annotation: Set $Z(\tau)=z(T\tau)/T$, $V(\tau)=v(T\tau)$. Then $Z_\tau=V$ and $\int_0^1V=T^{-1}\int_0^Tv=0$. In Equation (4.9), the primitive becomes $T\int_0^\tau\Omega(Ts)V(s)\,ds$. The rescaling therefore leaves the velocity, $c$ and source amplitudes unchanged, and changes the skew coefficient to $T\Omega(T\tau)$.

sec4.coercivity-constant|TorusEuler.Pape.annotation: In Equation (4.8) the right side controls the physical derivative, whereas Theorem A.1 asks for control of the derivative of the label displacement. Read Equation (4.6) in the direction $\|\xi_t\|_2^2\ge\|v\|_2^2/[D_-^2(1+\|M\|_\infty)^2]$. The factor $1/2$ from (4.8) then gives exactly the displayed mixed coercivity constant.

r2.s34.endpoint-unique-proof|TorusEuler..annotation: If two solutions of Equation (4.9) have the same $L$, their velocity difference $w$ satisfies $\mathcal R(K-J\Omega)w=0$ with $w=\mathcal Rw$. Coercivity gives $\mu\|w\|_{L^2_{a,t}}^2\le0$. Hence $w=0$; the initial trace determines the displacement, and the orthogonal spatial decomposition of (4.9) determines the difference of $c$ and the pressure gradient to be zero. No scalar pressure normalization is needed for this uniqueness statement.

sec4.polynomial-scale|TorusEuler.Paper.P.annotation: Let $S$ be the sum in Equation (4.10). Since $D_-\ge1$, we have $S\ge1$. The fixed-time reciprocal ellipticity is at most $S^2$ and the reciprocal path coercivity is $2D_-^2(1+\|M\|_\infty)^2\le8S^4$. The coefficient terms in $Q$ grow at most linearly in $S$. Therefore $Q\le CS^4$; raising to the fixed power of Appendix A gives (4.10) with an enlarged absolute exponent.

sec4.smooth-force-proof|TorusEuler.Paper.annotation: The smoothness clause is applied on the normalized slab to $L(T\tau,a)$. Composition with the linear change of time preserves smoothness, and the rescaling of $z$ then preserves smoothness on the original slab. This supplies the differentiability needed for Equation (4.11), including the one-sided time derivatives at the endpoints.

r2.s34.smooth-solution-proof|TorusEuler..annotation: In `solve42` the high-regularity part is supplied by Theorem A.1 on the rescaled slab. Its proof first lifts the spatial regularity of the whole path and then uses Equation (A.9) to bootstrap in time. Only joint smoothness of the displacement is retained at this step of the formal proof; `smooth42` uses its time derivative to reconstruct the instantaneous pressure and physical equation.

sec4.differentiate-integrated|TorusEuler.annotation: The derivative of the integrated left side is $Kv_t+K_tv-\Omega v-g$, since $L_t=-g$. The linked lemma assumes that the derivative of the integrated gradient is $-\nabla_a\mathsf q$; the smooth-data argument supplies such a derivative. Now $K_t-\Omega=\mathcal D$ gives Equation (4.11), with the force on the right.

Differentiate the spatially projected equation: $\mathbb P(Kv_t+K_tv-\Omega v-g)=0$. The smooth complementary field $g-(K_t-\Omega)v-Kv_t$ is a gradient. Its normalized periodic potential is $\mathsf q$ in Equation (4.11); the time regularity of any initially chosen scalar $\phi$ is immaterial.

sec4.piola|TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S34A.smo.annotation: The divergence constraint is preserved by the vector pushforward $B=Fv$. For $\det F=1$, Piola gives $(\operatorname{div}_x b)\circ X=\operatorname{div}_a v=0$; there is no separate spatial divergence condition on the components of $B$ in labels. Thus the same solenoidal constraint used in Equation (4.9) is sufficient for Equation (4.12).

r2.s34.freeze-kinetic-coefficient|TorusE.annotation: For fixed $t$, the parameter in Lemma A.2 is $2+D_-^2+\|K(t)\|_{C^1}$. Its fixed power is bounded by a fixed power of the parent sum in Equation (4.10), uniformly in $t$. Enlarging the absolute constant and exponent makes the same $A$ valid for both the fixed-time and the whole-path solves; it does not require the latter coercivity hypothesis for the fixed-time solve itself.

sec4.fixed-inverse-proof|TorusEuler.Pape.annotation: Here the inverse is applied to a projected datum $\mathbb Pf$. In `fixedTime42` the bounds for $K$ and its first label derivative are $K_0$ and $K_1$; the torus Lipschitz constant is at most $2K_1$. With ellipticity $D_-^{-2}$, the bound on the composite is $C_2(2+D_-^2+K_0+2K_1)^{p_2}\|\mathbb P\|$. Unlike the inverse for the whole endpoint problem, this estimate needs no lower bound on the displacement energy Equation (4.7).

r2.s34.common-inverse-bound|TorusEuler.P.annotation: The same coefficient bound $A$ in Equation (4.10) controls the endpoint solve and the inverse at a fixed time. For the force problem put $g=(D_aX)^T(f\circ X)$. The integrated source $L(t)=-\int_0^t g(s)\,ds$ obeys $\|L\|_{C_t C^{0,1/2}}\le T\|g\|_{C_t C^{0,1/2}}$. Applying the endpoint bound gives $\|v\|_{C_t C^{0,1/2}}\le AT\|g\|_{C_t C^{0,1/2}}$.

r5-B-purpose-central-gradient|TorusEuler.annotation: The next wave does not use merely a lower bound for $|\nabla U|$. It uses the particular matrix $\nabla U_{j-2}+\sigma E_2\otimes E_1$ in the preceding wave’s frame. The bound in Equation (5.50) controls every entry of the difference from this matrix; truncation adds one more small matrix in Equation (6.5).

r5-B-purpose-next-coercivity|TorusEuler..annotation: For a parent with residual $R_U$, the matrix in the endpoint problem is $H^\#=(D_x^2p_U-D_xR_U)\circ X$, not just the pressure Hessian. The new pressure is recomputed after truncation, and Equation (5.57) bounds the change caused by both $R_V$ and the Fourier tail. The new residual derivative is estimated separately in Section 7 using its finite frequency support.

c8-first-mean-cancels-parent-residual|To.annotation: The old error is removed in the first mean, not by the cutoff or the next wave's oscillatory equation. Indeed $\bar f_2+f_2=-H_2-R_U\circ X$, so the two new linear equations together cancel precisely those terms, with the supplementary source canceling the newly introduced phase advection. This is the cancellation used in Equation (5.29).

s5.parent-data|TorusEuler.Paper.S5.Paren.annotation: The parent is an approximate solution. To construct the next wave we need the band and deformation bounds (5.1) to differentiate its coefficients, the upper bound (5.2) to solve the mean equation, and a sufficiently small inherited residual Equation (5.6). In `Parent` the pressure need only be smooth and periodic, with an odd, band-limited residual satisfying these bounds. The zero-mean Poisson pressure used in the paper is a particular admissible choice and additionally makes $R_U$ divergence free.

s5.parent-frequency|TorusEuler.Paper.S5..annotation: At step $j$, the preceding cutoff gives a band $2\lambda_{j-1}^5$. Bernstein and the bound $\|U_{j-1}\|_\infty\le\lambda_{j-1}$ give $\|\nabla U_{j-1}\|_\infty\le C\lambda_{j-1}^6$. Thus $\mathsf D=\lambda_{j-1}^9$ covers both the band and the gradient for large initial frequency. The deformation bound is a separate part of Theorem 7.1 (T2), proved using Lemma 5.10 rather than Bernstein.

s5.even-coefficients|TorusEuler.IsLabelF.annotation: Both $M$ and $F=D_aX$ are even in $a$. Hence the inverse transpose is even and so is $\kappa=F^{-T}k_*$. The sign change of the phase $k_*\cdot a$ under reflection is not a sign change of its physical gradient. In particular the projection in Equation (5.4) and the seed equation are the same at the labels $a$ and $-a$.

s5.residual-fourier-band|TorusEuler.pare.annotation: All Fourier coefficients of $U$ outside $2\mathsf D$ vanish identically in time, so their time derivatives vanish as well. The tensor $U\otimes U$ has band $4\mathsf D$; both the divergence and the projection preserve that band. This is why the residual has a Bernstein bound even though no separate bound on $U_t$ is imposed in Equation (5.1).

s5.parent-coercivity|TorusEuler.Hierarch.annotation: The parent-geometry constructor takes Equation (5.2) as a hypothesis: it gives $H^\#=-(M_t+M^2)\le I$ along every particle. Neither finite Fourier support nor the strain bound supplies this inequality. For the initial stationary shear in Equation (6.1), $M_t=M^2=0$, so $H^\#=0$; for a later approximate solution one instead uses the pressure increments and the gradient of its residual.

s5.origin-normalization|TorusEuler.Paper.annotation: Positive rescaling of a nonzero solution of Equation (3.2) leaves its frame and all ratios of its lengths unchanged. It therefore leaves both conditions (5.5) unchanged. The paper chooses the scale to make $\max\gamma=1$; `Origin` requires only nonvanishing and $\gamma(t)\le1$.

s5.weight-and-coupling|TorusEuler.hasDer.annotation: In the moving frame $E_1=\kappa/|\kappa|$, $E_2=\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|$, the first coupling is $\nu=E_1\cdot ME_2$. In particular $\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a=\nu|\kappa||\mathbf a|$. This is the scalar whose positivity will give the sign of the leading pressure tensor in Equation (5.51). The amplitude weight $\gamma$ here is unrelated to the frame coefficient of the same name in the frame equations.

s5.envelope-plateau|TorusEuler.radialEnv.annotation: Every derivative of $g$ of positive order vanishes in the plateau. The central seed and covector are therefore unchanged by the spatial localization. In particular $g(0)=1$ in the computation of the rank-one central gradient Equation (5.50). The divergence completion and all other corrections are accounted for separately in its error term.

s5.leading-profile|TorusEuler.Paper.S5.l.annotation: At $x=0$ the term differentiating $g\mathbf a$ vanishes since $F_h(0)=0$; the term differentiating the phase is $\mathbf a\otimes\kappa$ since $g(0)=F_h'(0)=1$. This matrix has norm $|\mathbf a||\kappa|$, and its square is zero by transversality. It is precisely the added shear that enters the central comparison for the next wave; Equation (5.50) bounds the remaining gradients.

s5.central-transverse-assumptions|TorusE.annotation: The second inequality of Equation (5.5) is needed even if the transverse inverse is already controlled. The localized coupling has positive sign, so the coefficient $c_{\mathbf a}=2\widetilde\chi g(\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a)/|\kappa|^2$ is nonnegative. The leading pressure tensor is $-c_{\mathbf a}F_h'\kappa\otimes\kappa$, and its positive part is bounded by $Chc_{\mathbf a}|\kappa|^2I$. The factor $h$ changes the scale $\mathsf D^3\lambda^{1/4}$ to $\mathsf D^3\lambda^{-1/4}$, which is small enough to sum in the pressure bound.

s5.parent-smallness|TorusEuler.Hierarchy.annotation: The source of the first mean contains $-R_U\circ X$ and the phase average of the quadratic wave terms in Equation (5.25). The identity $\partial_s(C_2\cdot\kappa)=-\mathbf d\cdot V_1$ gives, after integration by parts, $\langle H_2\rangle=\mathbf d\cdot\langle V_1\otimes V_1\rangle$. Thus the derivative falls on the stress at fixed phase: it costs only a parent power, not $\lambda/h$. With $V_1$ of size $\lambda^{-5/4}$, the mean source has scale $\lambda^{-5/2}$, explaining the required size of the inherited residual.

s5.parent-smallness|TorusEuler.Paper.S5..annotation: If $r=\|R_U\|_{C_tL^\infty}>0$, Equation (5.6) imposes the upper restriction $\lambda\le r^{-2/5}$ on the new frequency. The correction estimates impose a lower restriction. At step $j$ the preceding residual has already been made at most $\lambda_j^{-3}$, so the upper endpoint is at least $\lambda_j^{6/5}$. Thus the preceding step must be designed with the next frequency already in mind.

r5-B-uniform-exponents|TorusEuler.Paper..annotation: There are two separate uniformity issues: the radius weights prevent a new parent power at each derivative, and the induction prevents a new parent power at each level. In Equation (5.40) the source and $\lambda^{1/2}B_p$ are bounded by the level scale without a factor $\mathsf D^C$. The mean estimate (5.35) is stronger than this induction bound by a factor $\lambda^{-1/12}$ before parent powers. The same reserve in the worst transverse product pays for the inverse and coefficient costs, so they are not multiplied through all $P$ levels.

r5-B-no-order-growth-assumption|TorusEul.annotation: At step $j$, the order $q_{j+1}$ is selected using the bound $\mathcal B(q_{j+1})\le\lambda_{j-1}$ in Equation (7.8), before setting the depth using $K_{j+1}$. Even rapidly growing fixed-order constants can be accommodated by leaving $q_j$ unchanged for more steps. Each fixed derivative order is eventually reached because $q_j\to\infty$.

p5.1.coefficient-list|TorusEuler.paperPr.annotation: In Equation (5.16), $\lambda\partial_s\mathsf p=(\lambda^2/|\kappa|^2)(\kappa/\lambda)\cdot(f-2MV)$. The two normalized coefficients of Proposition 5.1 therefore allow $\lambda\mathsf p$ to be estimated by the same norms as the force and transverse velocity, using the zero-mean phase primitive. The pressure is one power of $\lambda$ smaller than the velocity estimate; no derivative in the labels has been lost.

p5.1.polynomial-coefficients|TorusEuler..annotation: In `ParentLabelJetBound` the exponent is $pm+q$: $p$ is the cost of one further derivative, $q$ the cost before any derivative is taken. Thus the coefficient bound has $q=C$ while the composed-field estimate has $q=0$ and a separate amplitude $A_f$. This distinction survives summation in Equation (5.8).

The order-dependent constants are chosen from the assumed jet-bound constants before choosing $f$ or its amplitude. Thus Equation (5.7) can be applied to both $\nabla U$ and $R_U$, using their own supremum norms as $A_f$. The assertion is for every finite order, with one absolute exponent, not a bound on the growth of $C_m$ with $m$.

p5.1.composition|TorusEuler.Paper.Statem.annotation: Apply Equation (5.7) first with $f=\nabla U$, whose amplitude is at most $\mathsf D$, and later with $f=R_U$, whose amplitude is at most $\lambda^{-5/2}$. The derivative cost after transport is the same in both cases; their different sizes are preserved. This is why the residual does not require a separate composition calculus.

p5.1.weighted-coefficients|TorusEuler.Pa.annotation: The constants in Equation (5.8) may grow arbitrarily with order. Section 7 chooses the depth via a slowly increasing sequence $q_j$ so that $\mathcal B(q_{j+1})\le\mu=\lambda_{j-1}$. With $\mathsf D=\mu^9$ and $\lambda=\mu^{320b(q_j+1)}$, the relevant cost satisfies $\mathcal B(q_{j+1})\mathsf D^b\le\mu^{10b}\le\lambda^{1/32}$. This is how fixed-order estimates with an absolute exponent can be used at increasing depth.

p5.1.bernstein-input|TorusEuler.Paper.Li.annotation: Since $\nabla U$ has band $2\mathsf D$, a derivative of it costs $C\mathsf D$ by Equation (B.1). Thus $|U|_2\le C\mathsf D^2$ follows from the first bound of Equation (5.1), without a bound on $U_t$. Repeating at order $k-1$ gives the factor $\mathsf D^k$ for the velocity derivative in a $k$-block term of the chain rule.

p5.1.faa-di-bruno|TorusEuler.iteratedFDe.annotation: A partition into $k$ blocks describes which of the $n$ derivatives fall on each copy of $X$ in $U\circ X$. The block sizes $n_i$ sum to $n$. Removing the one-block partition leaves $k\ge2$ and hence $n_i<n$ for every block. Consequently every flow factor on the right of Equation (5.9) has already been bounded in the induction on $n$.

p5.1.jacobian-power|TorusEuler.norm_iter.annotation: A derivative of order $m$ of $F=D_aX$ is obtained from the flow jet of order $m+1$, with its last argument regarded as the vector on which the resulting linear map acts. The exponent becomes $5(m+1)-4=5m+1$. In particular the order-zero bound for $F$ agrees with Equation (5.1).

p5.1.residual-weighted|TorusEuler.exists.annotation: Bernstein on the $4\mathsf D$ band gives $|R_U|_m\le C_m\mathsf D^m\|R_U\|_{C_tL^\infty}$. The weighted composition estimate (5.8) cancels the derivative powers without enlarging the residual amplitude, giving Equation (5.10). Thus even the extra label derivative of $R_U\circ X$ needed for Equation (5.12) costs only an order-dependent constant times $\lambda^{-5/2}$. The mean estimate does not require $R_U$ to be localized in the envelope.

p5.2.mean-equation|TorusEuler.PaperSmoot.annotation: Put $F=D_aX$ and let $\xi$ be the first variation of the parent trajectory under the added velocity. Then $\xi_t=M\xi+B$; writing $\xi=Fz$ and using $F_t=MF$ gives $z_t=F^{-1}B$. The endpoint conditions amount to $\int_0^T F^{-1}B\,dt=0$ at each label. They concern the first variation of the final particle position; they neither set $B(T)$ to zero nor prescribe the final position of the full perturbed flow. (For the displacement identity, see Equation (4.4).)

p5.2.mean-coordinate-readout|TorusEuler..annotation: To transform Equation (5.11), put $B=Fv$ and multiply by $F^T$. Then $F^T\mathbf d\bar q=\nabla_a\bar q$ and $F^T(B_t+MB)=Kv_t+2F^TF_t v$. This gives Equation (4.11) with $g=F^T\bar f$, whose time primitive is the datum in Equation (4.9).

p5.2.source-derivative-loss|TorusEuler.p.annotation: For a derivative $w=\partial_a^\beta g$, the bounds $|w(a)-w(b)|\le2\|w\|_\infty$ and $|w(a)-w(b)|\le\|\nabla w\|_\infty|a-b|$ give a half-Hölder bound using one further derivative. With the radius weights this yields Equation (D.2), with factor $4\ell_*^{-1/2}$ in Lean. No time derivative of the force is required.

p5.2.all-solutions|TorusEuler.Paper.Stat.annotation: The phrase ‘every solution’ concerns pairs with the two displacement endpoints in Equation (5.11). Without the terminal condition the homogeneous equation could have nonzero initial velocity even for $\bar f=0$, contradicting Equation (5.12). It is this constraint that permits an estimate with only the force on the right, without an initial-data term.

p5.2.mean-estimate|TorusEuler.Paper.prop.annotation: In forming $H_p$ and its mean we have all orders of the earlier profiles available. Thus estimating $B_p$ at order $n$ by $\bar f_p$ at order $n+1$ consumes an estimate already proved, rather than requiring another equation for $B_p$. Its only appearance in the same-level transverse source is $-(B_p\cdot\kappa)\partial_sV_1$, which does not differentiate $B_p$. The formal statement admits the broader parent pressure class of Section 5.1.

p5.2.mean-coefficient-powers|TorusEuler..annotation: Put $F=D_aX$. The kinetic metric $K=F^TF$ and the skew coefficient $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$ involve only products of the already estimated parent coefficients. A derivative of order $m$ distributes among those factors with total order $m$. Thus Equation (D.6) persists with a fixed linear exponent in $m$, before the weights $\ell_*^m$ are applied.

p5.2.inverse-constant-power|TorusEuler.P.annotation: The constant $A$ in Equation (4.10) bounds the inverse of the two-endpoint equation. In its formula the inverse deformation and low-order norms of $M,K,\Omega$ are bounded by parent powers before choosing $\ell_*$. Choosing the radius afterward is important: the factor $\ell_*^{1/2}$ in Equation (5.13) must offset an inverse norm which does not itself grow as the radius shrinks.

p5.2.radius-threshold|TorusEuler.exists_.annotation: The derivatives of positive order have a small factor in Equation (D.7): $\ell_*^m|K|_m\lesssim_m\mathsf D^C\ell_*$, and likewise for $\Omega$. Passing to the half-Hölder norm costs $\ell_*^{-1/2}$ by Equation (D.2), leaving the factor $\sqrt{\ell_*}$. The formal coefficient bound makes this explicit as a parent factor $\mathsf D^9\sqrt{\ell_*}$, times order-dependent constants.

p5.2.radius-threshold|TorusEuler.Paper.S.annotation: For a label derivative, the highest derivative of $v$ still has coefficients $K$ and $\Omega$. Only terms in which at least one derivative falls on a coefficient are moved to the datum. Thus Equation (5.13) is a smallness condition on positive-order weighted coefficient derivatives; it does not require the metric $K$ or the skew term $\Omega$ to be small.

p5.2.radius-threshold|TorusEuler.Paper.T.annotation: At first order the new term in the datum is $(\partial_aK)v$. Applying the inverse after weighting it by $\ell_*$ costs at most $C A\ell_*|K|_{1,1/2}\|v\|_{[0],1/2}$. By Equation (5.13) this is bounded by an absolute multiple of the preceding order. At higher orders the inverse factor $A$ is similarly paired with the weight belonging to the derivatives that fall on $K$.

p5.2.radius-threshold|TorusEuler.Paper.P.annotation: One can see the remaining radius factor directly: Equation (D.7) at order $m$ and $m+1$ bounds the two terms on the right of Equation (D.2) by $C_m\mathsf D^C\ell_*$. Multiplication by $\ell_*^{-1/2}$ leaves the half power of $\ell_*$. The final scalar inequality absorbs $A$ after its bound has been obtained.

p5.2.mean-lifting-coefficients|TorusEule.annotation: The equation being differentiated is $Kv-\int_0^t\Omega v+L=c+\nabla_a\phi$. Its new datum at first order is $\partial_aL+(\partial_aK)v-\int_0^t(\partial_a\Omega)v$. The integral has norm at most $T\le1$ in $C_tC^{1/2}$; applying the solenoidal projection changes only a fixed operator constant. Both coefficient commutators therefore fit the same lifting estimate (see Lemma D.3).

p5.2.holder-estimate|TorusEuler.Paper.St.annotation: The input of the integrated inverse is $L=-\int_0^t g$, so the estimate (5.14) is for the same label Hölder order of $v$ and $g$. At this stage no derivative has been lost. The conversion Equation (D.2) is made only afterward, when the right side is measured using suprema of derivatives; the left side can be reduced to that norm without an extra derivative.

p5.2.holder-estimate|TorusEuler.Paper.Te.annotation: The velocity $v=F^{-1}B$ in Equation (5.14) has three label components and is solenoidal. This is the endpoint inverse on the whole slab, not the two-dimensional transverse inverse measured relative to the active seed. Its norm includes the Hölder seminorm at each derivative order through $n$. The Lean statement permits the broader parent pressure class under the residual and coercivity hypotheses.

p5.2.holder-estimate|TorusEuler.Paper.Pr.annotation: Writing $u_n=\|v\|_{[n],1/2}$, the commutator estimate gives $u_n\le C_n(A\|L\|_{[n],1/2}+u_{n-1})$. Indeed Equation (5.13) has already paid for the inverse acting on each differentiated coefficient. Induction from $u_0\le A\|L\|_{[0],1/2}$ therefore retains just one factor $A$; without (5.13) the naive recursion could lose a power of $A$ at each derivative.

p5.2.product-readout|TorusEuler.Paper.Pr.annotation: The two changes of coordinates are $g=F^T\bar f$ on the input and $B=Fv$ on the output. Each uses the same-order Hölder product estimate, and Equations (5.8), (D.2) bound the deformation factors. Neither change introduces an additional derivative of the unknown. The sole extra derivative of the source in Equation (5.12) comes from replacing its Hölder norm by a supremum norm.

p5.2.fixed-power-readout|TorusEuler.pape.annotation: The first inequality of Equation (D.2) bounds the output supremum norm by its Hölder norm without loss. The second bounds the input Hölder norm by $4\ell_*^{-1/2}\|\bar f\|_{[n+1]}$. Thus the extra derivative is on the known force alone, and $\ell_*^{-1/2}$ is a fixed parent power.

e02.transverse.weight|TorusEuler.paperHi.annotation: Here $\gamma(t)=\lambda^{3/4}|\mathbf a(t,0)|$ on $[t_0,T]$. By Equation (5.5), propagation from $t'$ to $t$ can cost a factor proportional to $\gamma(t)/\gamma(t')$. The weighted forcing norm controls the source relative to the seed at its time of application, not merely at the final time. No monotonicity of $\gamma$ is needed for the bound.

e02.transverse.equation|TorusEuler.Paper.annotation: Centering is necessary: averaging Equation (5.15) gives $\langle f\rangle_s=\partial_t\langle V\rangle_s+M\langle V\rangle_s$, since the pressure derivative integrates to zero. If $\langle V\rangle_s=0$, the force must have zero mean too. The normalized velocity and pressure are specified here; existence comes from the projected ODE.

e02.transverse.pressure-slope|TorusEuler.annotation: Use $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$ in the derivative of $\kappa\cdot V=0$. Then $0=-\kappa\cdot MV+\kappa\cdot(f-MV)-|\kappa|^2\partial_s\mathsf p$. The two identical strain terms account for the factor two in Equation (5.16). The nonzero wave vector makes division by $|\kappa|^2$ legitimate.

e02.transverse.projected-ode|TorusEuler..annotation: Write $P_\kappa$ for projection onto the normal line. If the force is entirely parallel to $\kappa$ and the velocity starts from zero, it produces only pressure, with $V=0$. For a general transverse velocity, however, the normal component of $V_t$ must be $P_\kappa MV$ because $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$. This accounts for the factor two in $-(I-2P_\kappa)MV$ rather than the instantaneous projection $-(I-P_\kappa)MV$. (For the homogeneous wave equation, see Equation (2.1).)

e02.transverse.activation-endpoint|Torus.annotation: The zero-start condition is at time zero. If $t_0>0$, vanishing of the force on the inactive prefix and continuity of the solution give $V(t_0)=0$; if $t_0=0$, this is the prescribed initial condition. The statement needed for Equation (5.21) is zero velocity at launch, not an independently imposed pressure value.

For positive $t_0$ the inactive condition gives zero at every earlier time, and continuity extends it to $t_0$. For $t_0=0$ there is no such earlier interval, so the conclusion instead uses the initial condition. This justifies dropping the launch contribution in Equation (5.20).

The joint smooth existence theorem preserves the vanishing prefix. In particular its velocity at the activation time is zero, by continuity for positive $t_0$ and by the given launch value when $t_0=0$. This is the property needed to pass from Equation (5.20) to the forced bound (5.21).

e02.transverse.frame-identities|TorusEul.annotation: The two identities express that $A_\perp^\dagger$ is a left inverse on the two coordinates and a projected inverse on the three physical coordinates. In particular $A_\perp^\dagger\kappa=0$. This lets one derive Equation (5.18) directly from Equation (5.15) without first substituting the formula for the phase pressure.

e02.transverse.frame-time|TorusEuler.Loc.annotation: The coefficient in the two-dimensional equation includes the derivative of the moving frame. Substituting $V=A_\perp v$ gives $V_t=A_\perp v_t+MA_\perp v$. Adding the strain $MV$ gives a second copy of $MA_\perp v$; multiplying by $A_\perp^\dagger$ kills the pressure direction and yields Equation (5.18).

e02.lemma53.near-origin|TorusEuler.Local.annotation: The coefficient of the principal Hessian of the leading pressure is $-c_{\mathbf a}F_h'$, where $c_{\mathbf a}=2\widetilde\chi g(\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a)/|\kappa|^2$. The sign in Equation (5.19) ensures $c_{\mathbf a}\ge0$. Thus the largest positive curvature from that tensor occurs where $F_h'$ is negative, and is bounded by $Chc_{\mathbf a}|\kappa|^2$. Positivity of the coupling is needed on the whole envelope, not just at its center.
