e02.lemma53.near-origin|TorusEuler.Paper.annotation: The seed hypothesis is relative: Equation (5.5) controls the propagation of every transverse vector at the origin, not just the selected seed. Together with the positive central coupling margin, it gives Equation (5.19) on a sufficiently small envelope. The numbered Lean statement permits an upper-normalized nonzero central seed rather than requiring the maximum to attain the normalization; it also admits the broader parent pressure class.

The pressure condition is an upper bound as a quadratic form, not a small norm of the Hessian. By Equation (5.19), $0\le c_{\mathbf a}|\kappa|^2\le2|\kappa||M||\mathbf a|\lesssim\mathsf D^3\lambda^{1/4}$. Since $F_h'\ge-Ch$ and $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$, its principal Hessian is bounded above by $C\mathsf D^3\lambda^{-1/4}I$. The linked numbered theorem establishes the seed bound and sign used here, with an upper-normalized nonzero central seed.

e02.lemma53.forward-hypotheses|TorusEule.annotation: Lemma 5.3(i) is an estimate for a given solution of the projected velocity equation with possibly nonzero launch data. Its support assumptions keep every label of interest within reach of the central propagator comparison. The active-profile theorem treats data on $[t_0,T]$ with compatible lattice-phase translations, without assuming a centered force.

The estimate in Lemma 5.3(i) does not require zero initial velocity or a centered forcing, because it concerns the projected ODE alone. The numbered Lean statement assumes full-slab smoothness and then estimates its active restriction; the related active-profile theorem covers data smooth only on the active interval.

e02.lemma53.forward-bound|TorusEuler.Hie.annotation: The term $\gamma(t_0)^{-1}\|V(t_0)\|_{[n]}$ permits two different applications of Equation (5.20). For the leading homogeneous solution the initial data have size proportional to $\gamma(t_0)$; for the forced correction the initial data are zero. The full-slab formal helper measures both on the active interval, and therefore yields the same type of estimate in each case.

e02.lemma53.forward-bound|TorusEuler.Pap.annotation: Integrating a bound using only $|M|\le\mathsf D$ could give an exponential in $\mathsf D$, too costly for the power-separated frequencies. Instead Equation (5.5) supplies a polynomial bound for the central propagator after dividing out the intended amplification. A small envelope transfers it to nearby labels. The numbered formal statement takes full-slab smooth data; the active-profile helper allows smoothness just on $[t_0,T]$.

e02.lemma53.zero-start-hypotheses|TorusE.annotation: The support condition puts the labels of the forced solution in the region where the central propagator estimate extends. The inactive-prefix condition gives $V(t_0)=0$, removing the launch term of Equation (5.20). Centering of the force has a separate role: it yields a centered velocity and a periodic pressure primitive. The mean correction is not required to share this support or time prefix.

r3c8-lemma53-transverse-existence|TorusE.annotation: The existence theorem produces the normalized pair with $V(0)=0$ and keeps the prescribed support and inactive prefix. It also has the phase-shift compatibility needed when the parent phase is not a lattice vector. The subsequent estimate in Equation (5.21) controls this pair quantitatively; existence itself is not the estimate.

After solving the velocity ODE there is no remaining freedom in the phase pressure. If two normalized pairs solve the same equation from zero, uniqueness for the velocity and Equation (5.16) give equality of the pressure derivatives; the average removes the integration constant. The linked result proves uniqueness, not existence.

e02.lemma53.transverse-pressure-bound|To.annotation: Equation (5.16) gives $|\partial_s\mathsf p|\le |\kappa|^{-1}(|f|+2|M||V|)$. The inverse wave-vector length provides the factor $\lambda^{-1}$, while taking the normalized phase primitive is bounded at the same scaled derivative order. In particular the pressure does not have to be obtained by inverting a spatial Laplacian on the torus at this step. The full-slab helper gives Equation (5.21) with exponent $20$.

The pressure estimate is later used together with the equation, not by differentiating it twice in physical space. At level two, $\mathsf p_2$ has size $\lambda^{-1-23/12}$ up to parent powers; two physical derivatives could leave $\lambda^{1/12}$. But $\kappa\partial_s\mathsf p_2=P_\kappa(f_2+f_2^S-2MV_2)$ has size $\lambda^{-23/12}$. Only one physical derivative is then needed, leaving $\lambda^{-5/12}$ in the Hessian bound (see Equation (5.52)). The numbered Lean estimate allows the broader parent pressure and central-amplitude hypotheses.

e02.lemma53.leading-bound|TorusEuler.Loc.annotation: The factor $h$ in Equation (5.22) is a bound on the phase profile, not on its slope at the origin. Indeed $F_h(0)=0$, $F_h'(0)=1$ and $g(0)=1$ give the central gradient $\mathbf a(t,0)\otimes\kappa(t,0)$ before switching. Thus the velocity can have size $\gamma\lambda^{-5/4}$ while its central gradient has scale $\gamma\lambda^{1/4}$ up to parent powers. The formal estimate uses a fixed admissible envelope.

e02.lemma53.leading-bound|TorusEuler.Pap.annotation: Lemma 5.3(iii) starts from a nonzero homogeneous seed, not from the zero-start inverse of Lemma 5.3(ii). The bound at launch is proportional to $\gamma(t_0)$, which cancels the launch denominator in Equation (5.20); multiplication by $F_h$ contributes $h$. The numbered formal statement fixes one admissible envelope instead of ranging over all cutoffs in the paper's class.

e02.lemma53.coframe-coefficient-proof|To.annotation: The Gram matrix $K_\perp=A_\perp^TA_\perp$ has eigenvalues between $\mathsf D^{-2}$ and $\mathsf D^2$. Differentiating $K_\perp^{-1}K_\perp=I$ bounds the jets of the inverse, and hence those of $A_\perp^\dagger$ and $\mathcal M_\perp$. These are bounds before multiplication by the radius weights; Equation (D.7) then absorbs the cost of each positive label derivative.

e02.lemma53.forced-integral|TorusEuler.w.annotation: Let $\Phi_a(t,t')$ denote the two-dimensional homogeneous propagator. The preceding estimate bounds $\Phi_a(t,t')$ by $e\mathsf D^3\gamma(t)/\gamma(t')$. Substituting this in the variation-of-constants formula gives Equation (5.23); the denominator in the integrand is $\gamma(t')$, not $\gamma(t)$. Thus even a very small early forcing is measured in relation to the early seed, and amplification from that time is already included.

e02.lemma53.near-seed-comparison|TorusEu.annotation: In the fixed coordinates, the difference $v_a-v_0$ has initial value $(A_\perp^\dagger(t_0,a)-A_\perp^\dagger(t_0,0))\mathbf a(t_0,0)$, and force $-(\mathcal M_\perp(t,a)-\mathcal M_\perp(t,0))v_a$. Both coefficient differences are bounded by a parent power times $|a|$. After applying Equation (5.23), return to the physical vectors by writing $\mathbf a(t,a)-\mathbf a(t,0)=A_\perp(t,a)(v_a-v_0)+(A_\perp(t,a)-A_\perp(t,0))v_0$. This retains the factor $|\mathbf a(t,0)|$. The Lean conclusion records the comparison with a coefficient depending on the parent bound.

The comparison is required relative to the central seed at every active time. This is what permits the initial projection and coefficient variation to be small even when the central seed is far below its terminal size. A uniform absolute error would not suffice to retain the positive coupling margin in Equation (5.5). The definition does not supply the bound on its comparison coefficient.

e02.lemma53.word-lifting|TorusEuler.Pape.annotation: Applying $\ell_*\partial_{a_i}$ to Equation (5.18) gives the same left-hand operator acting on $\ell_*\partial_{a_i}v$, with datum $\ell_*\partial_{a_i}\psi-(\ell_*\partial_{a_i}\mathcal M_\perp)v$. By Equation (D.7) the latter coefficient pays for the factor $\mathsf D^3$ of the zero-order inverse. A phase derivative has no such commutator. Higher mixed derivatives use this same argument with lower-order solutions.

e02.lemma53.pressure-coefficient-route|T.annotation: Rewrite $\lambda\partial_s\mathsf p$ as $(\lambda^2/|\kappa|^2)(\kappa/\lambda)\cdot(f-2MV)$. The two normalized coefficients have scaled bounds with no frequency power by Equation (5.8). Their product, followed by the zero-mean primitive of Lemma D.1, bounds the pressure without using a higher-order velocity estimate.

e02.lemma53.leading-proof-route|TorusEul.annotation: At $t_0$ the initial value for the homogeneous estimate is $g(I-P_\kappa)\mathbf a(t_0,0)$. Its scaled norm contains $|\mathbf a(t_0,0)|=\gamma(t_0)\lambda^{-3/4}$, so the small denominator in Equation (5.20) cancels. The factor $F_h$ contributes a further $h$ only after estimating $g\mathbf a$; this is the origin of $\lambda^{-5/4}$ in Equation (5.22).

e02.hierarchy.first-mean-source|TorusEul.annotation: The abstract pre-mean source at $p=2$ contains the material derivative of the stored completion of $V_1$, the slow gradient of its pressure and the two quadratic interactions. It subtracts the completion of the activation error at that level. With the cutoff identities this gives precisely the switched linear term in Equation (5.25).

e02.hierarchy.general-pre-source|TorusEu.annotation: At level three the slow products are $(Z_1\cdot\mathbf d)Z_2+(Z_2\cdot\mathbf d)Z_1$. The fast products are $(C_2\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY_2+(C_3\cdot\kappa)\partial_sV_1$. Both use only earlier oscillations and means, since $C_3=C[V_2]$. The linear terms carry the completion of $V_2$ and the slow gradient of its pressure to the next level. This is the general indexing in Equation (5.26).

e02.hierarchy.sources|TorusEuler.Paper.S.annotation: Adding the prescribed mean and transverse sources gives $\bar f_p+f_p=-H_p$ for $p\ge3$ and $-H_2-R_U\circ X$ for $p=2$. These are exactly the negatives of the known errors before the new mean starts transporting the earlier phases. The supplementary source then cancels the additional phase products. This split is the cancellation of the momentum residual through level $p$ in Equation (5.29).

e02.hierarchy.supplementary-source|Torus.annotation: The only new mean in Equation (5.28) occurs in $-(B_p\cdot\kappa)\partial_sV_1$; all differentiated oscillations are already known. It is important here that the mean has the improved bound. If $S_p=\lambda^{-5/4-2(p-1)/3}$, the ordinary level bound $B_p=O(S_p)$ would give a fast product of size $\lambda^{1/4}S_p$ up to parent powers. The stronger induction bound $O(\lambda^{-1/2}S_p)$ instead gives $\lambda^{-1/4}S_p$. The phase mean of the product is zero.

The indices of the fast mean interactions satisfy $i+j=p+1$, $i\ge2$, $j\ge1$. The allowed pairs can therefore be enumerated by $2\le i\le p$, with $j=p+1-i$. The endpoint $i=p$ pairs the current mean with $Y_1=V_1$; the linked equality is for the positive advection, so Equation (5.28) has a minus sign.

e02.hierarchy.transverse-after-mean|Toru.annotation: The new mean enters the transverse equation only in the now known supplementary force. Both $f_p$ and $f_p^S$ are centered, and the preceding oscillations make their sum vanish outside the envelope and on the inactive prefix. Thus the zero-start transverse inverse can be applied once to the entire force, with the pressure determined afterward by Equation (5.16). There is no coupled same-level iteration.

e02.hierarchy.order-required|TorusEuler..annotation: For fixed $p$, every $Y_{p+1-i}$ in Equation (5.28) has index at most $p-1$. Thus at level three the supplementary source is $-(B_2\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY_2-(B_3\cdot\kappa)\partial_sV_1$. The second term needs the mean just obtained, but neither term needs $V_3$. The congruence lemma expresses precisely this dependence on previously computed oscillations.

The term with $i=p,j=1$ has assigned level $p+1-1=p$, even though $B_p$ has just been found. The first index can start at two because $B_1=0$. Expanding the fast advection by the means on the diagonal $i+j=p+1$ gives the sum in Equation (5.28), with a minus sign when it is moved to the source side of the equation.

e02.prop54.well-defined|TorusEuler.Paper.annotation: At level $p$ the last correction already known is $C_p=C[V_{p-1}]$. It is the only level-$p$ field in $H_p$. The mean inverse applied to Equation (5.27) therefore determines $B_p$ before Equation (5.28) is formed; the transverse inverse and curl then determine $V_p,\mathsf p_p,C_{p+1}$. This also shows that increasing the final depth does not change the lower levels. The formal proposition asserts existence of the seed and uniqueness for fixed seed and normalized pressures.

e02.prop54.velocity-pressure-sums|TorusE.annotation: The phase derivative of $\bar q_p$ vanishes. The phase derivative of $\mathsf p_p$ enforces $\kappa\cdot V_p=0$ in Equation (5.15), while its label gradient is left for the next level. In particular the label gradient of $\mathsf p_P$ remains in Equation (5.30), even though $\mathsf p_P$ is included in the pressure sum.

e02.prop54.divergence|TorusEuler.Paper.S.annotation: With $V_0=V_{P+1}=0$, Equation (3.6) gives $\widetilde{\mathbf d}\cdot Z_i=\mathbf d\cdot V_i-\mathbf d\cdot V_{i-1}$ for $1\le i\le P+1$. Here the slow divergence of the curl $C_i$ and of the mean $B_i$ are both zero. Summing telescopes, with $Z_{P+1}=C_{P+1}$ providing the last cancellation. The proof uses the equivalent sum of completed curls.

e02.prop54.residual|TorusEuler.Paper.Sta.annotation: The residual of the parent is a function of $(t,a)$ alone after composition with $X$. It belongs entirely to the mean source at level two, with sign $-R_U\circ X$ in Equation (5.27). Its cancellation in Equation (5.29) is therefore pointwise in the independent phase as well as on the physical graph. The next residual consists only of the tail and the activation term.

e02.prop54.vanishing-prefix|TorusEuler.P.annotation: For $p\ge2$ the transverse correction vanishes at $t_0$: by the vanishing prefix if $t_0>0$, and by its initial condition if $t_0=0$. In Equation (5.20) the term $\gamma(t_0)^{-1}\|V_p(t_0)\|_{[n]}$ is therefore zero. At the level of the iteration this same exact vanishing eliminates all sufficiently late oscillations on any fixed interval before $T_\infty$, which is how Proposition 8.1 obtains convergence of high derivatives.

e02.prop54.tail|TorusEuler.hierarchyTail.annotation: The index square is filtered by $i+j-\mathrm{shift}>P$. Taking shift zero for label advection and one for phase advection gives the two thresholds in Equation (5.30). In the fast case the first index can start at two because $C_1=B_1=0$. The filtration is a finite-sum identity; the estimates for those products come later.

r2.prop54.level-cancellation|TorusEuler..annotation: The two equations in `IsExpansion` have separate right sides because the inverse for $B_p$ uses displacement endpoints while that for $V_p$ uses zero initial velocity. Adding them restores the full $-H_p$ and the supplementary source, along with the parent residual cancellation at level two. This is the termwise momentum cancellation used in Equation (5.29).

e02.prop54.surviving-levels|TorusEuler.h.annotation: The filtration groups each product by the integer $i+j-\mathrm{shift}$. Subtracting the sums for levels $2$ through $P$ leaves exactly the two tails in Equation (5.30). This applies to arbitrary summands; the expansion equations identify the terms to subtract.

r2.prop54.endpoint-citation|TorusEuler.P.annotation: The parent need not solve Euler exactly. The endpoint inverse uses $H^\#=(D^2p_U-\nabla R_U)\circ X$, the coefficient of the displacement equation, and its quadratic form enters with a minus sign in the coercive energy. The upper bound $H^\#\le\mathrm{Id}$ suffices on $T\le1$. This is the reason for carrying both a pressure-Hessian bound and a residual-gradient bound to the next step (the parent hypothesis in Equation (5.2)).

r5-B-linear-curl-estimate|TorusEuler.Pap.annotation: The part of the previous linear momentum not yet used is the momentum of $C_p=C[V_{p-1}]$ and the slow gradient of $\mathsf p_{p-1}$. This is exactly the first line of Equation (5.26). Lemma 5.5 gives an estimate for their sum using only the spatial norms of the preceding velocity and its forcing. For the first relay the unswitched homogeneous wave is used instead.

e02.lemma55.completion|TorusEuler.Paper..annotation: The estimate uses the normalized covector, its normalized reciprocal squared length, and the inverse deformation in the slow curl. Their scaled derivatives are controlled by Equation (5.8). The weight $\gamma^{-1}$ commutes with the spatial operators, so the same bound holds even during the small-amplitude part of the launch interval.

e02.lemma55.momentum-hypothesis|TorusEul.annotation: Use the momentum equation to eliminate $V_t$ before estimating $Q_t$. The potentially fast pressure term disappears since $\kappa\times(\kappa\partial_s\mathsf p)=0$. The remaining label pressure gradient is estimated separately from Equation (5.16); its centered primitive also has the factor $|\kappa|^{-1}$. The relay thus needs $f$ at one higher spatial order, with no time derivative of $f$.

e02.lemma55.relay|TorusEuler.Paper.State.annotation: For $V_p$, $p\ge2$, the source in Equation (5.32) is $f_p+f_p^S$. The left side is precisely the linear contribution sent to $H_{p+1}$, or to $R_P$ at $p=P$. Its exponent is $-5/4-2(p-1)/3-1$, which is $1/3$ below the required exponent at level $p+1$. Thus the relay can be estimated using the same source and velocity bounds, without losing a time derivative or enlarging the level cost.

e02.lemma55.unswitched|TorusEuler.Paper..annotation: At level two use $A_1$ in Equation (5.32), which solves the homogeneous equation on $[t_0,T]$. Using $V_1=\widetilde\chi A_1$ would instead introduce the forcing $\widetilde\chi'A_1$. Those switch derivatives belong to $R_{\widetilde\chi}$, leaving the homogeneous relay multiplied by $\widetilde\chi$ in $H_2$.

e02.lemma55.potential-frequency|TorusEul.annotation: Set $k=\kappa/\lambda$. Then $Q[V]=-\lambda^{-1}(k/|k|^2)\times\partial_s^{-1}V$, because $k$ is independent of $s$. The normalized coefficient $k/|k|^2$ has scaled label norms controlled by Equation (5.8); differentiation of it does not cost an additional power of $\lambda$. The slow curl of this expression retains the same prefactor.

r2.lemma55.parent-product-proof|TorusEul.annotation: Factor $\lambda^{-1}$ out of $Q[V]$. Use Equation (D.5) for its phase primitive and Equations (D.4) and (5.8) for the normalized coefficients. Applying the slow curl via Equation (D.3) costs one label derivative and $\ell_*^{-1}$, another fixed power of $\mathsf D$. These are the estimates combined in the proof of Equation (5.31).

The all-order coefficient bounds are needed here: if the $n$-th coefficient derivative cost an additional parent power for every $n$, the exponent in Equation (5.31) would grow with $n$. Proposition 5.1 uses the small label scale to avoid that. The proof `lemma55_main` combines those bounds with the primitive and curl estimates.

e02.lemma55.potential-time|TorusEuler.ha.annotation: Since $Q[V]=\partial_s^{-1}(-r\kappa\times V)$ with $r=|\kappa|^{-2}$, differentiate the three factors at fixed $(a,s)$. Substitution of $\kappa_t=-M^T\kappa$ and $V_t=f-MV-\kappa\partial_s\mathsf p$ gives $-r_t\kappa\times V+r(M^T\kappa)\times V+r\kappa\times(MV-f)$. Here $r_t=2(\kappa\cdot M\kappa)|\kappa|^{-4}$. The centered primitive commutes with time differentiation; this is Equation (5.33).

e02.lemma55.potential-time|TorusEuler.wa.annotation: `wavePotentialTimeSource` is the expression inside the phase primitive in Equation (5.33). It is centered because the coefficients depend only on $(t,a)$ and both $V$ and $f$ are centered. Its primitive is fixed by zero phase mean, so there is no additional function of $(t,a)$ to estimate in $Q_t$.

r2.lemma55.relay-product-proof|TorusEule.annotation: The differentiated coefficient of the potential still has degree $-1$ in $\kappa$: the last term of Equation (5.33) contains three covector factors and a denominator $|\kappa|^4$. The same degree occurs in Equation (5.16) for $\partial_s\mathsf p$. The primitive estimate and a single label derivative therefore leave $\lambda^{-1}$ in every term of the relay. Taking a direct bound on $\partial_t V$ would not exhibit this gain.

e02.lemma55.no-time-derivatives|TorusEul.annotation: In Equation (5.33) the forcing is evaluated at the current time. For the relay from $V_p$, the contribution of the newly solved mean enters through $f_p^S$ and hence algebraically through $B_p$. This avoids the need to estimate $\partial_t B_p$ using the endpoint equation. The smoothness of the profiles justifies differentiation; the quantitative induction needs only the label and phase norms.

e02.hierarchy.spare-frequency|TorusEuler.annotation: At level two the fast term with $C_2$ costs $\lambda^{3/2}\lambda^{-9/4}\lambda^{-5/4}=\lambda^{-2}$, up to parent factors. The target at that level is $\lambda^{-5/4-2/3}=\lambda^{-23/12}$. The difference is $1/12$. The exponent lemma is the same calculation for $i+j=p+1$, where the first generating velocity has index $i-1$. Choosing a decrement of $3/4$ would exhaust the gain of this interaction; the retained margin pays for the parent and depth constant in the smallness condition of Equation (5.43).

After each solve the auxiliary bounds may carry a parent factor, but the next source is estimated using Equation (5.40), which carries none. For each surplus $\delta\ge1/12$, $\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-\delta}\le1$. Absorbing this factor before starting the next level is what lets one use a single exponent $C$ at every depth; it does not require the numerical constants of the levels to be uniform.

r2.thm56.all-orders|TorusEuler.Paper.Pro.annotation: The only current-level unknown on the source side of Equation (5.28) is the already solved $B_p$, multiplying $\partial_sV_1$. Thus the order-$n$ transverse estimate needs only order $n$ of the new mean. The derivative loss in obtaining the mean is taken from earlier levels, which is why the finite expansion can use Equation (5.12) without a derivative-losing estimate for $V_p$ itself.

e02.thm56.level-bounds|TorusEuler.Paper..annotation: At $p=2$, the pressure bound alone gives $\mathsf p_2$ of size $\lambda^{-35/12}$. Two physical derivatives at cost $\lambda^3$ would yield $\lambda^{1/12}$. Instead (5.16) gives $\kappa\partial_s\mathsf p_p=P_\kappa(f_p+f_p^S-2MV_p)$, and the slow gradient costs only parent powers. The full pressure gradient has the scale $\lambda^{-23/12}$; one further physical derivative gives $\lambda^{-5/12}$ as in Equation (5.52). This is why the source is kept in Equation (5.34).

e02.thm56.level-bounds|TorusEuler.hierar.annotation: Write $e_p=-5/4-2(p-1)/3$. The base scale $e_1=-5/4$ comes from $\mathbf a$ of size $\gamma\lambda^{-3/4}$ times a profile of size $h=\lambda^{-1/2}$. The chosen decrement is $2/3$. The first omitted level has $e_{P+1}=-5/4-2P/3$, exactly the exponent in Equation (5.38).

e02.thm56.sum|TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.annotation:
The summed mean equation is linear over the same parent, so its physical divergence gives $\Delta\sum_p ar q_p^
atural=\operatorname{div}(\sum_p ar f_p)^
atural-2\operatorname{tr}(
abla U
abla ar W^
atural)$. The time derivative of the mean drops out by solenoidality. All fields on the right other than the fixed parent are phase independent, so physical differentiation costs only parent powers. This is why Lemma 5.9 uses the bounds for both sums in Equation (5.37) to control the mean pressure Hessian.

e02.thm56.advection-bounds|TorusEuler.Hi.annotation: The second term in Equation (5.39) has the slow derivative on the advecting field: $(\mathbf d\cdot Z)Z'$. This is the form produced by phase integration by parts in Equation (5.42). Its bound costs one label derivative of $Z$, but no factor $\lambda^{3/2}$.

e02.thm56.mean-induction-shift|TorusEule.annotation: With $e_p=-5/4-2(p-1)/3$, the sharp mean estimate is $\mathsf D^C\lambda^{e_p-7/12}$. The smallness hypothesis gives $\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-7/12}\le\lambda^{-1/2}$. This is the origin of the half-power in Equation (5.40): the extra mean decay survives even after removing the parent factor.

r2.thm56.parent-exponent|TorusEuler.Pape.annotation: For the numerical recurrence take $L$ to bound each primitive coefficient or inverse cost. Starting with the parent-free transverse source, the inverse gives $V_i$ a factor $L$, and the completion can cost $L^2$. A slow product of two such blocks, including its advection estimate, costs at most $L^5$. The mean inverse gives $L^6$; the smallness condition absorbs this factor before the new mean is used in Equation (5.28). This counts losses along the current level, not along all previous levels.

c8-hierarchy-solve-completion-step|Torus.annotation: The order-$n$ transverse bound (5.21) uses the source at order $n$, but the order-$n$ curl estimate (5.31) uses the velocity at order $n+1$. Thus (5.40) at order $n+1$ supplies the necessary bound to form $C_{i+1}$, including its extra $\lambda^{-1}$. There is no circular estimate involving the derivative of the new mean because Equation (5.28) contains it undifferentiated.

r2.thm56.level-block-definitions|TorusEu.annotation: At fixed level $i$, $Z_i$ has full divergence $\mathbf d\cdot V_i-\mathbf d\cdot V_{i-1}$. This is generally nonzero. The size blocks are chosen to estimate products; the solenoidal grouping instead pairs $V_i$ with $C_{i+1}$. The difference between these two groupings is essential in Equation (5.42), where the divergence of $V_{i-1}$ replaces phase differentiation of $C_i$.

e02.thm56.previous-completion|TorusEuler.annotation: For the mean the induction gives $\|B_i\|_{[n]}\lesssim\lambda^{e_i-1/2}$, with $e_i=-5/4-2(i-1)/3$ and the level constant understood. Since $Y_i$ vanishes before activation, its unweighted norm is at most its weighted norm on the active interval. Adding $B_i$ therefore gives the unweighted $Z_i$ bound in Equation (5.41). The mean need not obey the corresponding weighted bound.

e02.thm56.block-bounds|TorusEuler.Hierar.annotation: The hierarchy produced by the theorem bounds the two measured quantities $Y$ and $Z$ with the same frequency exponent and a common parent budget. Here the measured $Z$ is a sum of the weighted oscillatory norm and the unweighted mean norm, a stronger budget than the unweighted norm in Equation (5.41). It does not require the mean to vanish before $t_0$ or to be small relative to $\gamma(t)$.

e02.thm56.label-product-power|TorusEuler.annotation: In a slow product with $i+j=p$, the exponents add to $-5/2-2(p-2)/3=e_p-7/12$. The derivative acts at fixed phase, so it introduces no factor of $\lambda$. The same diagonal appears in the mean source after integration by parts in Equation (5.42), which explains why its target exponent in Equation (5.35) is the slow-product exponent rather than the fast-product exponent.

e02.thm56.fast-mean-integration|TorusEul.annotation: Integrate in the independent phase at fixed $(t,a)$: $\langle(C_i\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY_j\rangle_s=-\langle\partial_s(C_i\cdot\kappa)Y_j\rangle_s$. By Equation (3.6), $\partial_s(C_i\cdot\kappa)=-\mathbf d\cdot V_{i-1}$. Thus the averaged interaction contains a label derivative of $V_{i-1}$ and no fast derivative. Its indices now sum to $(i-1)+j=p$, rather than $i+j=p+1$. In particular at $p=2$ it has two leading-wave factors, just like the slow product.

e02.thm56.slow-mean-source|TorusEuler.Hi.annotation: At $p=2$ the only stress is $\langle V_1\otimes V_1\rangle_s$. Writing $A=\widetilde\chi g\mathbf a$, it equals $A\otimes A\int_0^1 F_h(s)^2\,ds$. The divergence differentiates $A$ at fixed phase and so costs no power of $\lambda$. Its two factors give $\lambda^{-5/2}$ up to parent factors. The term $R_U\circ X$ is included only at $p=2$ because it has the same permitted scale by Equation (5.10).

e02.thm56.mean-product-power|TorusEuler..annotation: The mean products have the same slow diagonal $i+j=p$, but each factor has the additional half-power in Equation (5.40). Hence their power is $e_i+e_j-1=-7/2-2(p-2)/3$, one full inverse frequency smaller than the averaged oscillatory products. Since $B_1=0$, there are no such products at $p=2$ or $3$.

e02.thm56.absorption|TorusEuler.hierarch.annotation: The mean source first has the power $e_p-7/12$. The mean inverse and absorption of the parent factor spend at most $1/12$, leaving the mean at $e_p-1/2$. Only then is the supplementary source estimated, at $e_p-1/4$ up to parent factors. Together with the centered source at $e_p-1/12$, it gives the parent-free transverse source in Equation (5.40). These are successive estimates of different quantities at the same level.

euler02.approximate.fields|TorusEuler.Hi.annotation: The pressure $\Pi$ is the one obtained in canceling the hierarchy. Since Equation (5.46) has a momentum defect, $\Delta\Pi=\operatorname{div}R_V-\operatorname{tr}((\nabla V)^2)$. Even if $V$ were left unchanged, its Poisson pressure would differ from $\Pi$ by a solution of $\Delta(p_V-\Pi)=-\operatorname{div}R_V$. Subtracting a spatial constant cannot remove this source. The pressure estimate after truncation must therefore account for the defect as well as the velocity tail.

euler02.approximate.common-exponent|Toru.annotation: The point of a depth-independent exponent is that Equation (5.43) must still hold at $P=6K_{j+1}$, not only at some fixed depth. In Section 7 the parent loss $\mathsf D^b$ becomes $\lambda_j^{9b/K_j}$ and the depth-dependent constant is bounded by the threshold at $q_{j+1}$. Enlarging the depth to reduce the remainder does not enlarge this exponent of the new frequency.

euler02.approximate.step-constant|TorusE.annotation: In step $j$, $\mathsf D=\lambda_{j-1}^9$ and $\Gamma_P\le\mathcal B(q_{j+1})\le\lambda_{j-1}$. Hence $C_{\rm step}\le\lambda_{j-1}^{9b+1}\le\lambda_{j-1}^{10b}$. In terms of the new frequency this is at most $\lambda_j^{10b/K_j}$, which is the parent loss to be absorbed in Equation (7.8).

euler02.approximate.constant-dependence|.annotation: The bound $C_{\rm step}=\Gamma_P\mathsf D^b$ is used for the fixed-order estimates that must be small at every step. For truncation we instead need the full velocity through the increasing order $P$. The factor $\mathsf D^{b(P+2)}$ in Equation (5.48) is allowed there because the cutoff supplies $\Lambda^{2-P}$ in Equation (5.55). The proof of Theorem 7.1 checks the balance between these two depth-dependent powers separately.

The two terms of the residual in Equation (5.46) both need two profile derivatives for the physical $C^{1,1/2}$ estimate. In the activation term these are derivatives of the completed field $A_1+C[A_1]$: Lemma 5.5 uses three derivatives of $A_1$ to control two of its completion. These are still fixed orders, so the coefficient of the residual need not depend on the arbitrary order $m$ of the velocity estimate.

euler02.approximate.smallness|TorusEuler.annotation: After fixing the parent and the depth, (5.43) amounts to $\lambda\ge(\Gamma_P\mathsf D^b)^{12}$. In the induction there is a stronger margin: $C_{\rm step}\le\lambda^{1/32}$ by Equation (7.8). It leaves, for example, the negative power $\lambda^{-7/32}$ in the one-sided pressure estimate (5.49).

euler02.approximate.graph-bounds|TorusEu.annotation: In the formal version the sum in Equation (5.44) runs over all ordered words of $m$ spatial directions. A multi-index $\beta$ occurs $m!/\beta!$ times in that sum, since the derivatives of the smooth evaluated field commute. The word bound therefore implies the displayed multi-index bound, and permits iteration of the one-derivative estimate without collecting multiplicities at each stage.

euler02.approximate.graph-unweighted|Tor.annotation: Taking the weight identically one gives a bound on the whole parent slab, rather than only on $[t_0,T]$. This is a change in the time supremum, not in the spatial differentiation operator: the factor $\lambda^{3m/2}$ in Equation (5.44) and the extra derivative for (5.45) are unchanged.

euler02.approximate.graph-mean|TorusEule.annotation: For the mean, $\widetilde{\mathbf d}f=\mathbf df$; all successive derivatives remain phase independent since the coframe has no $s$ dependence. Thus each derivative costs only a power of the parent bound, regardless of the new carrier. This accounts for the common frequency power $\lambda^{-5/2}$ at all orders of the mean in Equation (5.48).

euler02.approximate.holder-from-jets|Tor.annotation: For $d=|x-y|>0$, let $B_j,B_{j+1}$ bound the derivatives of orders $j,j+1$. The difference of the order-$j$ derivatives is at most $\min(2B_j,B_{j+1}d)\le\sqrt{2B_jB_{j+1}d}$. Dividing by $\sqrt d$ gives the half-Hölder seminorm. Taking $B_j,B_{j+1}\le B$ gives the linked bound $3(m+1)B$ on the sum of the supremum norms and seminorms through $m$. This explains the one extra ordinary derivative used in Equation (5.45).

euler02.approximate.mean-no-phase-cost|T.annotation: Applied to $\bar W$, the mean version of Equation (5.45) gives $C_{m,P}\mathsf D^{b(m+2)}\lambda^{-5/2}$ in Equation (5.48). The extra derivative needed for the half-Hölder seminorm increases the parent power but leaves $\lambda^{-5/2}$ unchanged. It is this fixed negative power of the new frequency, even at high spatial orders, that will control the nonoscillatory increments in Equation (7.4).

euler02.approximate.regularity|TorusEule.annotation: The matrix and coframe in the hierarchy are those of the actual flow of $U$, namely $M=\nabla U\circ X$ and $(D_aX)^{-T}$. Although the leading wave is chosen using the equations at the center, graph evaluation uses the full spatially varying coefficients. Consequently there is no additional error from replacing the parent by its linearization in Equation (5.46).

This equality reads out the two momentum sources from the assembled profiles, assuming their smoothness, parity, divergence and exact momentum identity in `PhysicalApproximationProperties`. It is the identity part of Lemma 5.8, not yet its estimate. The bounds on the hierarchy tail and the unswitched primary field enter only when estimating the two sources in Equation (5.48).

euler02.approximate.euler-residual|Torus.annotation: The residual here is the residual of the pair $(V,\Pi)$, not of $V$ with its zero-mean Poisson pressure. The record gives the exact identity (5.46); Equation (5.48) then estimates its right-hand side. The projection and change of pressure needed for the next parent occur only after truncation.

euler02.approximate.oscillation-sup|Toru.annotation: The estimate is for the oscillatory part of the same finite expansion that satisfies Equation (5.46). Its global supremum does not require a bound on its gradient. The subsequent estimate of the mean and the Fourier tail, rather than Equation (5.47), controls the rest of the increment in the prescribed derivative orders.

euler02.approximate.physical-estimates|T.annotation: The high-order bound on the oscillation is used in the opposite way from Equation (5.47): it need not be small, since it is multiplied by a Fourier-tail factor. At the chosen depth item 4 of the proof of Theorem 7.1 gives $1+\|V\|_{C_tC^{P,1/2}}\le3\lambda^{2(P+1)}$. In Equation (5.55) the cutoff $\Lambda=\lambda^5$ then gives $9\lambda^{5(2-P)+4(P+1)}=9\lambda^{14-P}$. With this bound, a cutoff at $\lambda^4$ would not yield decay with $P$. The extra power makes increasing the depth effective even after squaring the full velocity norm.

For $m=1$, (5.48) gives a frequency factor $\lambda^{7/4}$ because the Hölder estimate spends two graph derivatives. The first derivative alone has the sharper bound $\lambda^{1/4}$ from Equation (5.44). The extra loss is a convenient way of estimating the seminorm, not a new contribution to the gradient. The separate value and first-derivative bounds can also be interpolated to obtain spatial Hölder estimates of order below one.

The absence of a carrier cost does not mean that higher means have uniformly bounded derivatives in the parent scale. At step $j$, for $m\le q_j$, the coefficient $\mu^{10b(m+2)}$ is at most $\lambda^{1/16}$ by $K_j=320b(q_j+1)$ and $m+2\le2(q_j+1)$. Thus $\lambda^{-5/2}$ has ample decay left: the mean is bounded by $\lambda^{-3/2}$ through all the orders required at this step. The other part of Equation (7.4) is supplied by the Fourier tail.

Both residuals are estimated in $C^{1,1/2}$ by the order-two profile bound. Multiplication by $\lambda^3$ turns the hierarchy tail into $\lambda^{7/4-2P/3}$ and the switch term into $\lambda^{7/4}|\widetilde\chi'|\gamma$, apart from parent factors. Replacing $7/4$ by $2$ gives the common prefactor in Equation (5.48). The first estimate is unweighted on the entire slab; the second is needed only on the support of the switch derivative.

For each admissible cutoff the linked result supplies one expansion with all the bounds of Equation (5.48), as well as the pressure and central-gradient estimates. In particular the residual belongs to the velocity whose norms are estimated here. Its cutoff term retains the factor $\|\widetilde\chi'\gamma\|_\infty$; obtaining a small residual still requires the specific early switch of Section 6.

euler02.approximate.momentum-chain-rule|.annotation:
For the full velocity, the transport operator on the correction decomposes as $(\partial_t+U\cdot
abla)W^
atural+W^
atural\cdot
abla W^
atural$. The first term is a derivative at fixed $(a,s)$, and the second uses the physical graph derivatives. The remaining cross term $W^
atural\cdot
abla U$ is $(MW)^
atural$. This accounts for all terms in Equation (5.29).

euler02.approximate.parent-cancellation|.annotation: In label coordinates the parent source in the momentum equation is $R_U(t,X(t,a))$, independent of $s$. The hierarchy has been constructed with its negative as the level-two mean source. At the physical point $x=X(t,a)$ the two terms are literally equal with opposite signs; no estimate on $\|R_U\|$ is needed for their cancellation in Equation (5.46).

euler02.approximate.divergence|TorusEule.annotation: Exact divergence is needed before the frequency cutoff. The identity $\operatorname{div}W^\natural=(\widetilde{\mathbf d}\cdot W)^\natural=0$ preserves the localization of the oscillatory part without applying a spatial projection to it. A Leray projection of an approximately solenoidal localized wave could produce a nonlocal oscillatory correction, whereas the later limit argument uses exact vanishing outside a shrinking ball to obtain smooth spatial convergence away from the origin (Proposition 8.4).

euler02.approximate.sup-proof|TorusEuler.annotation: The weighted order-zero profile bound and $\gamma\le1$ give (5.47) with no carrier loss. In item 5 of the proof of Theorem 7.1 $C_{\rm step}\le\lambda^{1/32}$, hence $\|O_j\|_\infty\le\lambda_j^{-39/32}\le\lambda_j^{-1}$. The derivative bound on the rest of the increment is established separately.

euler02.approximate.cutoff-derivative|To.annotation: At a fixed time $\widetilde\chi^{\prime}(t)$ commutes with spatial derivatives. The $m=1$ case of Equation (5.45) costs $\lambda^3$, and the unswitched amplitude is bounded by $\lambda^{-5/4}\gamma(t)$ up to parent factors. This gives $\lambda^{7/4}|\widetilde\chi^{\prime}(t)|\gamma(t)$; enlarging $7/4$ to $2$ yields the second term in Equation (5.48).

Apply Equation (5.45) with weight one to $R_P$ and with weight $\gamma$ to the unswitched primary field. The factor $\widetilde\chi'$ depends only on time, so the spatial derivatives do not act on it. The supremum in Equation (5.48) is therefore of the product $|\widetilde\chi'|\gamma$ at the times of the switch.

r5-B-depth-remainder|TorusEuler.Paper.le.annotation: The depth is measured in powers of the current frequency but the required smallness is measured at the next one. Indeed $P=6K_{j+1}$ turns $\lambda_j^{-2P/3}$ into $\lambda_{j+1}^{-4}$. The early-amplitude estimate turns $e^{-L_j}$ into precisely the same next-frequency power. The remaining prefactors in Equation (5.48) and in the bound for the switch derivative are absorbed in Section 7, leaving the residual small enough to serve as the next parent defect.

r5-B-rank-one-after-activation|TorusEule.annotation: With the cutoff equal to one the leading increment is $\mathbf a\otimes\kappa$. In its moving frame it maps $E_1=\kappa/|\kappa|$ to $\sigma E_2$, $\sigma=|\mathbf a||\kappa|$, and kills $E_2,E_3$. The correction error in Equation (5.50) and the truncation error in Equation (5.56) must both be included in the next parent matrix.

euler02.pressure-flow.pressure-upper|Tor.annotation: By Equation (4.7), the displacement form is $\int(|\xi_t|^2-\xi\cdot H^\#\xi)\,dt$. An upper bound $H^\#\le\operatorname{Id}$ and $T\le1$ give a lower bound $\frac12\int|\xi_t|^2\,dt$ by Equation (4.5). Thus Section 7 sums the upper pressure increments and estimates the current residual derivative separately; large negative pressure curvature is not an obstruction to this argument.

The center coupling $\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a$ remains positive on the chosen label support by Equation (5.19). This extension of the sign, rather than positivity only at $a=0$, is needed for the Hessian bound on the whole torus. The time cutoff is nonnegative, and outside the active support the primary pressure coefficient is zero.

euler02.pressure-flow.primary-hessian|To.annotation: Write $c=c_{\mathbf a}\circ X^{-1}$ and $\theta=k_*\cdot X^{-1}$ locally on the supported cell. Differentiating $-cP_h(\theta)$ twice gives $-cF_h'\kappa\otimes\kappa-F_h(\nabla c\otimes\kappa+\kappa\otimes\nabla c+cD^2\theta)-P_hD^2c$. In Equation (5.51) the first term is the only one that differentiates the phase profile twice; the other terms vanish in the affine case with spatially constant coefficient and normal.

euler02.pressure-flow.primary-remainder|.annotation: Each of the four remaining tensors in Equation (5.51) contains at most one fast phase derivative; the others differentiate parent coefficients or the slow profile. Their total norm is bounded by $C\mathsf D^C\lambda^{3/2}\|\mathsf p_1\|_{[2]}\lesssim\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-3/4}$. The paper takes the primary pressure norm from Equation (5.22); the linked proof reads the same estimate for the actual hierarchy from Equation (5.34) at $p=1$.

euler02.pressure-flow.transverse-gradien.annotation: Take the scalar product of Equation (5.16) with $\kappa$. Differentiating $\kappa\cdot V_p=0$ gives $\kappa\cdot V_{p,t}=\kappa\cdot MV_p$, accounting for the second copy of $MV_p$. This yields the fast pressure gradient directly as $P_\kappa(f_p+f_p^S-2MV_p)$. At $p=2$ the bound is $O(\lambda^{-23/12})$ up to parent constants, whereas differentiating the pressure profile by Equation (5.44) alone would give $O(\lambda^{-17/12})$.

euler02.pressure-flow.higher-gradient-bu.annotation: For $p\ge2$, (5.34) bounds $\lambda\mathsf p_p$, $V_p$ and the sources at the same level rate. The slow gradient of $\mathsf p_p$ gains $\lambda^{-1}$ relative to that rate, up to parent factors; the phase gradient is recovered directly from Equation (5.16) at the level rate. Thus the sum of gradient profiles in $[1],\gamma$ has the level-two bound $C_{2,P}\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-23/12}$.

euler02.pressure-flow.higher-hessian|Tor.annotation: `HigherHessianClaim` is the bound in Equation (5.52) for the whole higher oscillatory pressure, with $p=1$ excluded. At level two the pressure scale is $\lambda^{-35/12}$. Paying twice for a physical derivative would give $\lambda^{1/12}$; recovering the first gradient from Equation (5.16) saves a factor $\lambda^{1/2}$ and yields the required decay.

The first gradient is already known as a profile, $G_p=\mathbf d\mathsf p_p+P_\kappa(f_p+f_p^S-2MV_p)$. Hence $D_x^2\mathsf p_p^\natural=D_xG_p^\natural$, and Equation (5.44) is applied only once. The level-two exponent changes by $3/2$, from $-23/12$ to $-5/12$; no favorable sign is required of these Hessians.

euler02.pressure-flow.mean-hessian|Torus.annotation: `MeanHessianClaim` is the norm estimate for the sum of the phase-independent pressures. Since the mean velocity and source in its Poisson equation are phase independent, their conversion to physical $C^{1,1/2}$ norms costs powers of $\mathsf D$ but no $\lambda^{3/2}$ factor. This leaves the rate $\lambda^{-5/2}$ from Equation (5.37).

euler02.pressure-flow.center-leading|Tor.annotation: Since the odd parent fixes zero, evaluation there means $a=0$, $s=0$ at every time. In Equation (3.1) the slow gradient of $\widetilde\chi g\mathbf a F_h$ carries the zero factor $F_h(0)$; the fast gradient carries $g(0)F_h'(0)=1$. This identifies the exact contribution of $V_1$ to Equation (5.50).

euler02.pressure-flow.center-intermediat.annotation: For the remainder, the $[1]$ norm controls the slow gradient and $h\partial_s$ of the oscillation. The physical gradient in Equation (3.1) therefore costs at most $O(\mathsf D^C\lambda^{3/2})$. At the level-two rate this leaves $\lambda^{-5/12}$, while the phase-independent mean needs no fast derivative. The difference between $-5/12$ and $-1/3$ is the frequency gain available for absorbing constants.

The rate $\lambda^{-5/12}$ is written as $\lambda^{-1/3}\lambda^{-1/12}$. The second factor pays for the parent and depth constants through Equation (5.43). This is why (5.50) has no step constant in front of its central error.

euler02.pressure-flow.center-smallness|T.annotation: The intermediate estimate is $C_{2,P}\mathsf D^C\lambda^{-5/12}$. Since $C_{2,P}\mathsf D^C\le C_{\rm step}$, the factor $C_{\rm step}\lambda^{-1/12}$ in Equation (5.43) is at most one. This leaves $\lambda^{-1/3}$, a bound with no parent-dependent prefactor, as required for the next frame comparison.

euler02.pressure-flow.deformation|TorusE.annotation: The estimate is uniform in the admissible solenoidal perturbation $v$, so in Section 7 it applies directly to the truncated child, not merely to the untruncated approximation. Both the deformation and its inverse are among the parent bounds in Equation (5.1). This is the reason for retaining polynomial control of both directions of the flow.

The bound is on both the forward deformation and the inverse matrix, not on $\nabla(V+v)$ or a small difference from the identity. The proof obtains bounded derivatives of a lifted flow and small derivatives of its label displacement in scaled variables. Restriction to the physical phase graph then introduces the growing factor in Equation (5.53).

euler02.truncation.residual-definition|T.annotation: The cutoff does not preserve the momentum equation, even when $R_V=0$: $u\otimes u$ need not equal $S_\Lambda(V\otimes V)$. The actual new defect in `residual` is the one for the recovered pressure. By Equation (5.58) its two sources are the projected filtered defect $\mathbb P S_\Lambda R_V$ and the projected divergence of this tensor difference.

euler02.truncation.velocity-properties|T.annotation: The velocity produced by the cutoff is the next parent, with frequencies at most $2\Lambda$. In particular the support bound in Equation (5.1) will be available with any $\mathsf D\ge\Lambda$. Bounds on the next gradient and deformation still require the estimates in the induction; the support bound by itself gives neither.

euler02.truncation.error-bounds|TorusEul.annotation: The $C_tC^{2,1/2}$ bound for $u-V$ is used in the flow estimate of Lemma 5.10 and the central-gradient estimate. The two terms in the second bound control the new defect and the change in pressure curvature. In the formal statement these last norms are bounded at two independently chosen times, which permits taking the two suprema separately as in Equation (5.56).

euler02.truncation.pressure-upper|TorusE.annotation: Add $D^2(p-\Pi)$, bounded in norm by Equation (5.56), to $D^2(\Pi-p_U)$, bounded above by Lemma 5.9. The large negative part of the latter need not be estimated. Keeping this distinction lets the pressure bound survive the cutoff even when the central shear of the new wave is large.

euler02.truncation.residual-identity|Tor.annotation: Since the cutoff commutes with the time derivative and the divergence, filter the momentum equation for $V$ and apply $\mathbb P$ to obtain $u_t+\mathbb P\operatorname{div}S_\Lambda(V\otimes V)=\mathbb P S_\Lambda R_V$. Subtract from the equation defining $R_u$; the time derivatives cancel. In the remaining tensor insert and subtract $V\otimes u$ and $V\otimes V$. This gives $(u-V)\otimes u+V\otimes(u-V)+(I-S_\Lambda)(V\otimes V)$, the three terms of Equation (5.58).

euler-r2.truncation.quadratic-tensor-cos.annotation: All three tensors in Equation (5.58) need a bound of order two, but only one factor in each mixed product needs to be small. The tail $v_\Lambda$ gives $\Lambda^{2-P}\|V\|_{C^{P,1/2}}$, and $u$ and $V$ are bounded by $C\|V\|_{C^{P,1/2}}$. For the last tensor apply the tail estimate directly to $V\otimes V$, whose high norm is quadratic in the same norm of $V$. Thus there is one tail factor, not two, in the common budget.

euler02.truncation.holder-product|TorusE.annotation: One uses (5.59) at order two for the tensor terms of Equation (5.58), because a divergence follows the product. In the pressure equation the products are of first derivatives of the velocities and the Hessian is recovered by an operator of order zero; there the product estimate at order zero suffices.

At order two the first mixed tensor in Equation (5.58) is bounded by $C\|v_\Lambda\|_{C^{2,1/2}}\|u\|_{C^{2,1/2}}$. Uniform boundedness of $S_\Lambda$ controls the second factor by the norm of $V$. The other mixed tensor has the analogous bound. One tail factor is sufficient; neither $u$ nor $V$ is required to be small in that norm.

euler-r2.truncation.tensor-estimate|Toru.annotation: In the last tensor of Equation (5.58) the cutoff acts after multiplication. First bound $\|V\otimes V\|_{C^{P,1/2}}$ by $C_P\|V\|_{C^{P,1/2}}^2$, then apply Equation (B.2) to the tensor itself with $s=2$. This produces the same tail factor as in the mixed terms. The divergence loses one derivative and the Leray projection is bounded on the remaining Hölder space.

e03-s6-shear-formulas|TorusEuler.station.annotation: The matrix in Equation (6.1) is the gradient at zero. At a general point it is multiplied by $\cos(2\pi x_2)$. In particular $DU_0(x)v=2\pi\cos(2\pi x_2)v_2(e_1+\rho e_3)$, so its image is contained in its kernel.

e03-s6-fixed-second-coordinate|TorusEule.annotation: The equation for the second particle coordinate is $\dot X_{0,2}=0$. Hence the velocity of each particle remains its initial velocity, and integration gives the affine-in-time trajectory in Equation (6.2).

e03-s6-square-zero|TorusEuler.stationary.annotation: The factor $e_2\cdot(e_1+\rho e_3)=0$ gives $B_\rho^2=0$. Thus $(I+cB_\rho)(I-cB_\rho)=I$ for every $c$, giving Equation (6.2) without an inverse-series estimate.

e03-s6-lemma61-origin|TorusEuler.paperLe.annotation: The first wave satisfies Equation (5.5) with room to spare: the relative propagation constant is at most $2$, and the first coupling is at least $\pi$. The same $\mathsf D\ge2$ therefore bounds the first quantity and the reciprocal of the second. The subsequent wave will require a much larger $\mathsf D$, because its seed undergoes both amplification and decay on the comparison interval.

e03-s6-lemma61-origin|TorusEuler.Paper.S.annotation: The two estimates in Equation (5.5) have separate uses. The relative propagator bound controls the inhomogeneous transverse equations in the expansion. The lower bound on $\nu$ gives $\kappa\cdot M\mathbf a=|\kappa||\mathbf a|\nu>0$ at the center, which is then extended to the envelope for the pressure estimate.

e03-s6-lemma61-origin|TorusEuler.Paper.l.annotation: The first wave needs only comparable lengths on a short interval. The reflection $I-2P_\kappa$ has norm one, so the logarithmic derivative of the length of any nonzero solution has absolute value at most $|B_\rho|$. This gives the relative bound of Equation (5.5) without using the growing-mode analysis.

e03-s6-positive-first-coupling|TorusEule.annotation: The loss from $2\pi$ is at most $2t|B_\rho|^2\le |B_\rho|/4\le\pi$. The resulting $\nu\ge\pi$ is stronger than the $\mathsf D^{-1}$ needed in Equation (5.5).

e03-s6-normalized-shear|TorusEuler.Movin.annotation: The factors $S^{-1}$ in Equation (2.3) occur in complementary coordinates of $k$ and $\mathbf a$, so that $k\cdot\mathbf a=(\lambda/S)\zeta\cdot\alpha$. The scaled transverse variables have comparable components at launch, although the growing physical amplitude has an $E_1$ component of order $S^{-1}$ times its $E_2$ component. Here $S$ is a dimensionless shear parameter, not the final time $S_j$ of §7.

e03-s6-growing-initial-direction|TorusEu.annotation: In the strong-shear system at $\tau=0$, $\alpha_1'=-\alpha_2$ and $\alpha_2'=-\alpha_1$. The vector $(-1,1)$ belongs to the growing eigendirection. Undoing the scaling in Equation (2.3) gives $-E_1/S+E_2$, which is perpendicular to the chosen launch normal $E_3$.

e03-s6-physical-comparison-error|TorusEu.annotation:
The four terms of Equation (2.6) are the relative changes of $B_{12}$ and $B_{32}$, $\|B\|_\infty/r$, and $\|E_c\|_\infty/
u$. Differentiate the entries in the moving frame: their derivatives have norm at most $4\|B\|_\infty^2+\|B_t\|_\infty$. Integrating this bound and dividing by the smaller entry $\eta$ controls both relative changes. The denominator $
u$ for $E_c$ comes from the scaling of the amplitude equations ($S/r=1/(2
u)$), so smallness merely relative to the shear strength would not suffice.

e03-s6-frame-speed|TorusEuler.MovingWave.annotation: Each frame equation in Equation (2.2) contains two entries of $B$. Their absolute values are at most $\|B\|_\infty$, so $|E_i'|\le2\|B\|_\infty$. In $B_{ij}'=E_i'\cdot BE_j+E_i\cdot B_tE_j+E_i\cdot BE_j'$ this gives $4\|B\|_\infty^2+\|B_t\|_\infty$. The time derivative of the moving matrix entry is therefore different from that of $B$ in a fixed frame.

r2-s6-reference-turn|TorusEuler.MovingWa.annotation: The reference turning time is at least $2/\varepsilon$, whereas the cutoff has completed by normalized time one. A crossing in the stated bracket therefore gives both the target coupling ratio and the full preceding shear for the next step. Its strength is estimated by Equation (2.23), which uses the product of the amplitude and the now longer wave vector.

e03-s7-central-couplings|TorusEuler.Pape.annotation: The first coupling in Equation (7.1) is an entry of the older gradient in the frame of the new wave. Its bound at $t_{j+1}$ gives the next frozen value of $\nu$. The lower bound throughout $[t_j,S_j]$ has a different use: it keeps the leading pressure coefficient nonnegative at the center and, after localization, on the envelope.

e03-s7-half-length|TorusEuler.paperTheor.annotation: The two halves of $[t_j,S_j]$ play different roles. The first contains the crossing, and the second leaves enough of the parent slab for all subsequent launches, since each subsequent allowance is at most a quarter of the preceding one (Equation (7.7)). In fact the total length of all future launch gaps is at most $4\tau_j/3$, whereas the active interval has length $2\tau_j$.

e03-s7-depth|TorusEuler.InductiveEulerPa.annotation: To make the depth factor in Equation (5.38) of size $\lambda_{j+1}^{-4}$, solve $2P/3=4K_{j+1}$. This gives $P=6K_{j+1}$, which also leaves enough decay for the derivative factors and Fourier truncation. `stepDepth` uses the shifted index $i=j-1$; thus it reads the order $q_{i+2}$.

e03-s7-T4-splitting|TorusEuler.paperTheo.annotation: The full rank-one term has norm $\sigma_j$ at the crossing and becomes the preceding shear of Equation (6.5). It is not enough to approximate that matrix to a small relative error: the scaled amplitude equation multiplies the central error by $S/r=1/(2\nu)$, not by $1/\sigma$. The absolute tolerance $\lambda_j^{-1/4}$ therefore keeps the comparison error small even when the leading matrix grows without bound.

e03-s7-oscillation-support|TorusEuler.Pa.annotation: Fourier truncation is nonlocal in space. The compact support retained by the finite oscillatory profiles is therefore assigned to their physical evaluation $O_j$ before truncation. The difference produced by the multiplier is included with the mean in the remainder of Equation (7.4).

e03-s7-inactive-oscillation|TorusEuler.P.annotation: For $j\ge2$, $O_j(0)=0$. The phase-independent correction is solved with zero displacement at both ends, which is not zero velocity at both ends. Its initial value can therefore change $U_j(0)$; Equation (7.4) makes these changes, including the Fourier errors, summable at every fixed spatial order.

e03-s7-all-orders|TorusEuler.frequencySc.annotation: Fix $m$ first. Once $q_j\ge m$, all subsequent remainders in Equation (7.4) are bounded in $C_tC^{m,1/2}$ by $\lambda_j^{-1}$. Choosing a later index so that $t_j\ge T$ gives the same estimate for the full increments on $[0,T]$ when $T<T_\infty$.

r5-ind-figure4-inactive|TorusEuler.Paper.annotation: The solid part of each row is the interval where the oscillation is absent; the mean is already defined there and may change the initial velocity. The solid segment therefore marks where the full increment has the high-order estimate of Equation (7.4), not where the two successive velocity fields agree.

e03-s7-low-gradient|TorusEuler.exists_pa.annotation: The spatial Bernstein bound costs one power of $\Lambda_j=\lambda_j^5$ and gives $C\lambda_j^6$ for the gradient. To estimate $\partial_t\nabla U_j$, take one spatial derivative in Equation (7.5). The quadratic term now contains two derivatives and the Leray projection is bounded in $C^{0,1/2}$; using a third ordinary derivative to control this Hölder norm costs $C\Lambda_j^3\lambda_j^2=C\lambda_j^{17}$. Together with the small differentiated residual this fits $\lambda_j^{18}$. The Hölder step avoids using an $L^\infty$ operator bound for the projection.

e03-s7-half-length-decay|TorusEuler.freq.annotation: By Equation (1.15), $\tau_j\le\mu^{-1/8}(\log\mu)^6\le\mu^{-1/16}$ for large $N$. At $j+1$ this gives $4\tau_{j+1}\le4\lambda_j^{-1/16}\le4\mu^{-1/4}\le\mu^{-1/8}\le\tau_j$. The last inequality uses $L_{j+1}\ge1$. Both estimates are uniform because $\mu\ge N$.

e03-s7-growth-rate|TorusEuler.activation.annotation: The square root in $r=\sqrt{2\sigma\nu}$ turns the strength bounds at the preceding crossing into $c\mu^{1/8}\le r\le C\mu^{1/8}L_j$. Consequently $2r\tau_j$ is between $2cL_{j+1}^3$ and $CL_jL_{j+1}^3\le CL_{j+1}^4$. The lower estimate allows the required crossing, and the upper one limits the polynomial loss in Equation (2.7).

e03-s7-error-budget|TorusEuler.induction.annotation: The first term of Equation (6.6) bounds the variation of the moving-frame couplings relative to $\eta=\nu\varepsilon$. The length $2\tau_j=2\mu^{-1/8}L_{j+1}^3$ multiplies a bound $C\mu^{1/16}$ for $\|B\|^2+\|B_t\|$. This yields $C\varepsilon^{-1}L_{j+1}^3\mu^{-1/16}$. The older gradient divided by $r$ costs $C\mu^{-3/32}$, and the central error divided by $\nu$ costs $C\mu^{-1/4}$. Both latter denominators are bounded below by the inherited crossing values.

r2-s7-comparison-smallness|TorusEuler.Pa.annotation: For the fixed constant $C_0$ in Equation (2.7), $C_0\varepsilon\le C_0(\log N)^{-2}$, and $C_0(2r\tau_j)^{C_0}\delta/\varepsilon\le C\mu^{-1/16}(\log\mu)^{8C_0+14}$. Each bound tends to zero uniformly in $\mu\ge N$ as $N$ grows. The threshold thus does not have to be chosen again at each comparison.

e03-s7-switch-residual|TorusEuler.exists.annotation: The derivative is confined to the first normalized unit. There $\gamma\le e^{3-L_j}$ and $|\widetilde\chi'|\le Cr$, so $\|\widetilde\chi'\gamma\|_\infty\le Ce^3\mu^{1/8}L_j\lambda_{j+1}^{-4}\le\mu\lambda_{j+1}^{-4}$. The last inequality follows from Equation (1.15), uniformly in $j$. Wave one contributes no switching residual.

e03-s7-depth-residual-identity|TorusEule.annotation: The factor $\lambda^{-2P/3}$ is the remainder *before* the physical derivative and coefficient costs in Equation (5.48). Solving $2P/3=4K_{j+1}$ gives $P=6K_{j+1}$, hence the same next-frequency power $\lambda_{j+1}^{-4}$ as the exponential smallness from switching on the wave.

e03-s7-residual-power|TorusEuler.frequen.annotation: The two errors inside the parentheses of Equation (5.48) are bounded by $\lambda_{j+1}^{-4}$ and $\mu\lambda_{j+1}^{-4}$. With the physical derivative cost $\lambda^2$ and $C_{\rm step}\mu\le\lambda^{1/16}$, their contribution is at most $2\lambda^{2+1/16}\lambda_{j+1}^{-4}$. At the next frequency this loses at most half a power, since $\lambda_{j+1}^{1/2}=\lambda^{K_{j+1}/2}$ dominates $2\lambda^{2+1/16}$. The resulting $-7/2$ leaves room for the constant in Proposition 5.11 before imposing the $-3$ residual allowance.

e03-s7-wave-coefficient-cost|TorusEuler..annotation: A derivative in physical space may differentiate the phase, at cost $|\kappa|/h\lesssim\mathsf D^2\lambda^{3/2}$. The oscillatory $C^{P,1/2}$ estimate in Equation (5.48) uses $P+1$ derivatives at this scale and starts at size $\lambda^{-5/4}$. Including the coefficient bound gives exponent $3(P+1)/2-5/4+(P+2)/32=(49P+10)/32<2(P+1)$. The mean estimate is smaller, so both fit the full-depth bound used for truncation.

r2-s7-new-truncation|TorusEuler.Paper.Th.annotation: The velocity $V$ is the exactly divergence-free field obtained from the finite expansion. The new parent is $U_j=S_{\Lambda_j}V$, and its pressure is computed afresh from $\Delta\pi_j=-\operatorname{tr}((\nabla U_j)^2)$. If $v_\Lambda=U_j-V$, then $U_j-U_{j-1}=O_j+\bar W^\natural+v_\Lambda$. The last two terms, rather than the oscillation itself, will have small high-order norms. This is the decomposition used in Equation (7.4).

r3c8-s8-derivative-strategy|TorusEuler.P.annotation: There are two ways to remove the oscillatory tail. On $[0,T]$ for $T<T_\infty$, the activation times eventually lie after $T$. On $[0,T_\infty]\times K$ for $K$ away from zero, the shrinking supports eventually miss a neighborhood of $K$. In either region only $U_j-U_{j-1}-O_j$ remains in the late increments, and Equation (7.4) sums its derivatives once $q_j$ exceeds the desired order.

e03-s8-initial-data|TorusEuler.Inductive.annotation: The first two activation times are both zero, but only the first cutoff is identically one. The second oscillation vanishes at its activation time, as do all later ones at time zero. Thus the initial datum is built from the first truncated wave and the sum of the later mean and Fourier corrections (summable at every fixed spatial order by the second bound in Equation (7.4)), not by prescribing the stationary shear as the final initial datum.

e03-s8-initial-smooth|TorusEuler.PaperLi.annotation: The uniform limit on the closed slab defines both $w(0)$ and $w(T_\infty)$. The additional preactivation vanishing at $t=0$ upgrades the first of these limits to every fixed spatial order. At the terminal time the corresponding upgrade from Equation (7.4) is local, on compact sets separated from the shrinking supports of the oscillations.

e03-s8-initial-smooth|TorusEuler.Paper.P.annotation: The convergence in each $C^{m,1/2}$ uses a possibly different starting index, chosen once the scheduled orders reach the desired regularity (Lemma 1.3 of the main paper), but the sequence and its limit are unchanged. Compatibility of the limits follows from their common order-zero limit. Thus the construction gives a single smooth initial field, rather than a family of initial fields each with only a prescribed finite regularity.

e03-s8-bounded-velocity|TorusEuler.Paper.annotation: The global velocity estimate involves no sum of gradients. At the level of Equation (5.44), the oscillation has size $\lambda_j^{-5/4}$ and a first derivative bounded by $\lambda_j^{1/4}$, up to parent powers. The frequency grows much faster than the parent factors. This explains how the former estimate gives summability while the central derivative, whose lower bound requires the separate projection argument, can grow without bound.

e03-s8-central-curl|TorusEuler.paper_sec.annotation: On $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$ the preceding cutoff has already become one. The new curl, in contrast, is multiplied by a cutoff that varies during this interval. One must avoid subtracting its magnitude in the lower bound for the sum. Projection onto the instantaneous direction of $\kappa_j$ kills the new leading curl for every value of the cutoff, while the preceding curl has a positive component in that direction by the wave-vector comparison in Lemma 2.4, which bounds the corresponding component of the new scaled wave vector below by one half.

e03-s8-central-curl|TorusEuler.Paper.Sta.annotation: In Equation (8.2) the retained curl is at least $c\mu^{1/8}$, where $\mu=\lambda_{j-1}$. Dividing the right side of Equation (8.2) by $\mu^{1/8}$ gives at least $c-C\mu^{-3/32}-C\mu^{-1/8}$, since $\lambda_{j-2}^9\le\mu^{1/32}$. This stays positive for all sufficiently large $j$. The order-one tail estimate then transfers the bound to the limiting curl with a vanishing additional error.

e03-s8-rank-one|TorusEuler.coordinateCur.annotation: For the linear field $v(x)=\mathbf a(\kappa\cdot x)$, the gradient is $\mathbf a\otimes\kappa$ and $\operatorname{curl}v=\nabla(\kappa\cdot x)\times\mathbf a=\kappa\times\mathbf a$. This fixes the sign in Equation (8.1); the reverse cross product would give the opposite surviving component.

r2-s8-geometry-before-projection|TorusEu.annotation: The frame is the moving frame of the preceding pair, not the fixed frame at launch. Put $\Theta=r(S_j-t_j)$. In the scaled coordinates (2.3) the window bounds give $|\zeta_1|\le\Theta^2$, $|\zeta_2|\le\Theta$, $1/2\le\zeta_3\le3/2$. Since the physical components of $\kappa_j/\lambda_j$ are $(\zeta_1,\zeta_2/S,\zeta_3)$, its norm is at most $3\Theta^2$ for $S,\Theta\ge1$. Thus the cosine with the preceding curl direction $E_3(t)$ is at least $1/(6\Theta^2)$ throughout the window. The bound $\Theta\le CL_{j+1}^4$ gives Equation (8.1).

In item 2 of the proof of Theorem 7.1 the rate is $r\le C\mu^{1/8}L_j$, where $\mu=\lambda_{j-1}$, and the reserved time is $S_j-t_j=2\mu^{-1/8}L_{j+1}^3$. Their product is at most $CL_jL_{j+1}^3\le CL_{j+1}^4$. The wave-vector length bound is quadratic in this normalized time, giving the $L_{j+1}^8$ loss in the projection. The frequency power $\mu^{1/8}$ cancels when computing the normalized window.

e03-s8-maximal-and-integrals|TorusEuler..annotation: The rate is frozen at launch. With $r=\sqrt{2\sigma\nu}$, the upper strength bound in Equation (7.3), not the lower one, gives $r\le C\lambda_{j-1}^{1/8}L_j$. The crossing's normalized delay is at least $2L_j^2$, so division by the upper rate leaves $\lambda_{j-1}^{1/8}(t_{j+1}-t_j)\ge cL_j$. This is the lower time weight paired with the vorticity estimate.

e03-s8-off-origin|TorusEuler.PaperTermin.annotation: The velocity traces on different compact sets are restrictions of the same globally continuous $w(T_\infty)$. The time-derivative traces agree on overlaps by uniqueness of their order-zero limits. Thus the conclusion gives well-defined spatial fields on the punctured torus for velocity and its first time derivative, but not a limit of every time derivative. The latter needs bounds for every fixed mixed space-time derivative of the nonoscillatory increments (Lemma 1.2 of the auxiliary note).

r5-term-oscillation-support|TorusEuler.P.annotation: The oscillation $O_j$ is the evaluated profile before Fourier truncation. The parent flow fixes zero and takes its label support of radius $2\ell_*$ into a ball of radius at most $2\mathsf D\ell_*\le2\mathsf D^{-2}\le\lambda_{j-1}^{-1}$. Fourier truncation itself does not preserve spatial support; the nonlocal difference $v_{\Lambda_j}$ is included with the mean in the second bound of Equation (7.4).

e03-s8-shrinking-support|TorusEuler.indu.annotation: Put $d=\operatorname{dist}_{\mathbb T^3}(K,0)>0$. For late $j$, the ball of radius $\lambda_{j-1}^{-1}<d/2$ misses the open $d/2$ neighborhood of $K$, uniformly in time. On that neighborhood the entire increment equals $U_j-U_{j-1}-O_j$. This is why one can apply Equation (7.4) to its derivatives there even though the Fourier-truncated increment is not itself supported in the ball.

e03-r2-appa-symmetry|TorusEuler.Paper.St.annotation: For the parent flow these symmetries follow from $K=F^TF$ and $\Omega=F^T(M^T-M)F$. Skew-symmetry gives $\Omega w\cdot w=0$, but not $\Omega z_t\cdot z=0$. In the path problem the latter term represents the effect of the pulled-back vorticity on a displacement, and must be included in Equation (A.2).

e03-appa-primitive|TorusEuler.endpointPr.annotation: Integration in $J$ keeps the label fixed. Thus $z=Jv$ gives $z(0)=0$ without a further integration constant, and its other trace is $z(1,a)=\int_0^1v(t,a)\,dt$. The space in which we solve for $v$ consists of paths with this integral zero (the two displacement endpoints in Equation (4.9), after rescaling); it does not require $v$ itself to vanish at either end.

e03-appa-ellipticity-and-energy|TorusEul.annotation: To apply these inequalities to Equation (4.9), write $Z(\tau)=T^{-1}z(T\tau)$. Then $Z_\tau=z_t(T\tau)$ and $Z$ has both traces zero. Changing variables in the label energy and dividing by $T$ gives precisely the form (A.2) with $K(T\tau)$ and $T\Omega(T\tau)$. By Equations (4.6)–(4.7) one may take $\mu=[2D_-^2(1+\|M\|_\infty)^2]^{-1}$; Equation (A.1) holds with $\kappa=D_-^{-2}$. There is no inverse power of the slab length in either constant.

e03-appa-forcing-continuity|TorusEuler.P.annotation: On the normalized interval the inclusion $C_tC_a^{0,1/2}\hookrightarrow C_a^{0,1/2}(L_t^2)$ has norm at most one: apply $\|h\|_{L_t^2}\le\sup_t|h(t)|$ to the values and to each difference of label paths. Continuity of $L(t)$ in the stronger norm is used when the right-hand side of Equation (A.9) is formed.

e03-appa-a1-polynomial-estimate|TorusEul.annotation: For the higher-order mean estimates it is essential that Equation (A.3) has no source derivative. For example the source for $\partial_i v$ is $\partial_iL+(\partial_i K)v-J((\partial_i\Omega)v)$. Multiplying its estimate by $\ell_*$, the commutator contribution has coefficient at most $CA\ell_*(|K|_{1,1/2}+|\Omega|_{1,1/2})\le C$, by Equation (5.13). At order $m$ the same cancellation holds for every positive-order coefficient derivative with its factor $\ell_*^j$. The base inverse cost $A\le\mathsf D^C$ is thus not raised to a new power at each derivative order in Equation (5.14).

e03-appa-a1-smooth-conclusion|TorusEuler.annotation: For the parent flow $F_t=MF$, so $K_t-\Omega=2F^TMF=2F^TF_t$. With $L_t=-g$, differentiation of Equation (4.9) gives Equation (4.11) on taking $\mathsf q=-\phi_t$. Multiplication by $F^{-T}$ sends the label gradient to the physical pressure gradient along $X$, and the Piola identity transfers $\operatorname{div}_a v=0$ to $\operatorname{div}_x b=0$. Lean instead differentiates the projected equation and recovers the zero-mean pressure as a potential of the negative differentiated residual; it does not need to identify a particular $\phi_t$.

e03-appa-energy-identity|TorusEuler.endp.annotation: Since $(Jw)_t=w$, integration by parts gives $\int_I J(\Omega w)\cdot w=[J(\Omega w)\cdot Jw]_0^1-\int_I\Omega w\cdot Jw=-\int_I\Omega w\cdot Jw$. The boundary term vanishes because $Jw(0)=Jw(1)=0$, even though $J(\Omega w)(1)$ need not vanish. This recovers the plus sign of the second term in Equation (A.2).

r5-B-two-projected-inversions|TorusEuler.annotation: The two applications of Lemma A.2 have different ranges. With $H=L^2(I;\mathbb R^3)$ the projection is $\mathbb P\mathcal Q$ and the lower bound is Equation (A.2); this solves for all times with the terminal constraint. With $H=\mathbb R^3$ the projection is $\mathbb P$ and the lower bound is Equation (A.1); this solves for a solenoidal field at each time. The second inversion is made with the source recovered from the first, not with a fresh choice of endpoint data.

e03-appa-a2-base-isomorphism|TorusEuler..annotation: By Equation (A.5), $\mathcal RBv=0$ implies $v=0$. The range is also closed, since the estimate makes preimages of a Cauchy sequence of outputs Cauchy in the projected Hölder space. To prove that all projected data lie in the range, the paper starts with $B=I$, where this is true, and preserves surjectivity by continuation. `Paper.lemma_A_2` supplies the proved isomorphism in both the spatial and the path-valued cases.

e03-appa-a2-base-bound|TorusEuler.paperL.annotation: With $B=K(t)$ and $\mu=D_-^{-2}$, the cost in Equation (A.5) comes from the inverse deformation and the size and spatial variation of the metric $F^TF$. The concrete spatial theorem bounds the inverse by a degree-$145$ polynomial in these quantities. There is no derivative of the source in this estimate; the differentiated force in Equation (4.11) is used for a different purpose, namely recovery of the physical equation.

e03-appa-a2-base-bound|TorusEuler.Paper..annotation: The bound depends on the reciprocal of the lower quadratic-form bound and the size and spatial variation of $B$. The Lipschitz version replaces $\|B\|_{C^1}$ by $\|B\|_\infty+\operatorname{Lip}B$. It is important that the source needs only the half-Hölder norm: no derivative of it is spent in Equation (A.5).

The norm on the right of Equation (A.5) is the norm of the projected output, not of $Bv$. Taking $v=e^{-1}f$ in the estimate defining `FreezingConclusion` gives a bound for $\|e^{-1}f\|$ in terms of $\|f\|$ for projected $f$. This matters when the equation contains an unknown gradient or time-independent field, since neither needs to be estimated before solving for $v$.

e03-appa-a2-higher-isomorphism|TorusEule.annotation: The higher-order conclusion can be read as $v\in C^{k,1/2}$ if and only if $\mathcal RBv\in C^{k,1/2}$, under the stated regularity of $B$. In the forward direction use the product rule. In the reverse direction use the higher inverse and uniqueness of the base solution. The higher constants are not required to be the base constant in Equation (A.5).

In the higher-order clause of `FreezingConclusion` the map is the same equivalence $e$ as in Equation (A.5), with $v$ of higher regularity exactly when $ev$ has higher regularity. Bounds for both $\|ev\|_{C^{k,1/2}}$ and $\|v\|_{C^{k,1/2}}$ give continuity in the higher norm. This is how the formal statement expresses an isomorphism in that norm.

e03-appa-frozen-multiplier-bound|TorusEu.annotation: Both symbols $A_0^{-1}$ and $A_0^{-1}r$ give order-zero operators with the same type of half-Hölder bound. The first acts on $f$ in Equation (A.7); the second takes the unprojected coefficient errors as its inputs. The formal estimate takes $C_0\le C(2+\mu^{-1}+\|B_0\|)^{11}$, which controls the dependence on $B_0$ in the subsequent choice of the cutoff radius.

e03-appa-dyadic-kernel-decay|TorusEuler..annotation: Five integrations by parts at unit scale give decay $|y|^{-5}$, whereas inserting one frequency factor for a kernel derivative costs only a bounded factor on the annulus. Rescaling to $2^j$ gives $2^{3j}$ from volume and $2^{dj}$ from $d$ derivatives. The choice five is enough both for the integrable half-Hölder moment of the kernel and for summing the differentiated kernels away from the diagonal, which is needed for the far term of Equation (A.7).

e03-appa-zero-mode-bound|TorusEuler.norm.annotation: The annular blocks do not see the zero Fourier coefficient. Its output is $A_0(0)^{-1}\widehat f(0)$, with norm at most $\min(1,\mu)^{-1}\|f\|_\infty$. For mixed paths $r(0)=\mathcal Q$, not the identity. Bounding this constant term is needed for the supremum part of Equation (A.6), although it contributes nothing to the Hölder seminorm.

e03-appa-coefficient-continuation|TorusE.annotation: On the fixed space, $S_s=\mathcal RB_s=(1-s)I+sS_1$. One interpolates the coefficients, not the inverses. The operators along this segment have the same projection constraints, and their quadratic forms interpolate between the identity form and Equation (A.4). Hence the estimates proved for $S_1$ apply uniformly along the segment.

e03-r2-appa-fixed-time-inverse|TorusEule.annotation: The fixed space of the spatial Leray projection is the solenoidal half-Hölder space. The linked lemma identifies the compressed equivalence with an equivalence on that space with forward map $u\mapsto\mathbb P(K(t)u)$. Hence applying Lemma A.2 at each $t$ gives the inverse family used in Equation (A.9), with a common bound from the uniform coefficient and ellipticity estimates.

e03-appa-all-time-derivatives|TorusEuler.annotation: After obtaining continuity of $v$ in $C_a^{k,1/2}$, differentiate Equation (A.9) once to get $S(t)v_t=\mathbb P(\Omega v-L_t)-S_t v$. At order $m+1$, all terms on the right involve at most $m$ time derivatives of $v$: the derivative of the primitive is $\Omega v$, and the other terms arise by differentiating $S$ at least once. Inversion at the same spatial order gives the next time derivative without spending a label derivative. Doing this for each $k$ gives joint smoothness.

e03-appb-bernstein|TorusEuler.paperLemma.annotation: The residual has frequencies up to $4\Lambda$. Reproduce it with $S_{4\Lambda}$, whose symbol equals one on that entire band, then differentiate the reproducing kernel rather than the residual. Its order-$m$ derivative has $L^1$ norm $C_m(4\Lambda)^m$. This proves Equation (B.1) with the factor $4^m$ absorbed in the constant; the formal real-target version tests support against continuous linear functionals.

An ordered list of $m$ coordinate derivatives can represent the same multi-index in several ways. The linked complex Banach-valued estimate bounds the sum with these repetitions; dropping them gives Equation (B.1). A separate version proves the multi-index estimate for real normed targets.

e03-appb-uniform-constants|TorusEuler.pa.annotation: The constant in Equation (B.2) can be taken to dominate the finitely many absolute moments of the fixed kernel through order $M$, the Taylor and derivative-sum constants, and the operator bound for $s=M$. It is chosen before $f$ and $\Lambda$. Thus the cutoff cost at depth $M$ is eligible for the numerical threshold in Appendix C.

e03-appb-uniform-constants|TorusEuler.Pa.annotation: One fixes the constants from the symbol before choosing the frequencies. The $L^1$ mass gives the operator bound, derivatives of the kernel give $C_m$ in Equation (B.1), and a maximum over the finitely many moments through order $M$ and the operator bound gives $C_M$ in Equation (B.2). These can all be included in $\mathcal B$ before the schedule is chosen.

e03-r2-appb-kernel-dilation|TorusEuler.s.annotation: Under dilation the mass stays fixed, while derivatives and moments scale in opposite directions. In particular $\|\partial^\beta K_\Lambda\|_1=\Lambda^{|\beta|}\|\partial^\beta K\|_1$ and $\int |y|^k|K_\Lambda(y)|\,dy=\Lambda^{-k}\int |y|^k|K(y)|\,dy$. These are the two scale factors in Equations (B.1) and (B.2).

e03-appb-kernel-derivative-scale|TorusEu.annotation: The identity leaves the factor $(4\Lambda)^{|\beta|}$ when derivatives are moved to the kernel of the reproducing cutoff. Summing these bounds gives Equation (B.1), absorbing $4^{|\beta|}$ in $C_m$. The linked full lemma gives Bernstein, rather than stating the kernel identity separately.

r5-app-fixed-parent-power|TorusEuler.Pap.annotation: For the mean, differentiation of the integrated equation leaves a forcing term with a derivative on $K$ or $\Omega$.
